subtitle.text: The first Wednesday of every month was always a "Perfectly Awful Day" at the John Grier Home for Orphans.
That's when the trustees and the ladies' committee visited us.
Of course, we gave them tea and sandwiches.
But this was more than a social call.
These men and women were also inspecting us.
Everything at our orphanage had to be perfect.
There was so much work to do!
And as the oldest orphan, I—Jerusha Abbott—did most of it.
One Wednesday I was on my feet at five o'clock in the morning.
I mopped floors, dusted chairs, and made beds.
I helped to scrub and dress 97 squirming orphans.
I also reminded them to behave.
"If a trustee or lady speaks to you, what do you say?"
The children looked at each other and burst into giggles.
"You say, 'Yes, sir' or 'No, ma'am.'
Remember your manners and be polite to anyone you meet today."
Mrs. Lippett, the matron at the orphanage, rushed me through these extra chores.
She appeared calm to our guests.
But behind the scenes, she was often quite frantic.
This Wednesday, like all the others, finally dragged to a close.
As our guests were leaving, I returned to my regular duties in Room F.
I was in charge of eleven little girls, ages four to seven.
It was time for supper.
So I straightened their dresses and wiped their noses.
Then I sent them off to the dining room.
I stayed upstairs and sank into a window seat.
I pressed my aching head against the cool glass.
The day seemed like a success.
The ladies and gentlemen had made their rounds, read their reports, and sipped their tea.
From my seat, I watched their carriages and automobiles rolling out of the orphanage gates.
In my mind I followed them to the big houses dotting the hills.
I imagined myself riding home in one of those carriages.
I wore a fur coat and a velvet hat.
But then I tried to picture the inside of my imaginary house . . . and I couldn't.
That was because I'd never been in a real house in all my 18 years.
"Je-ru-sha Ab-bott, you are want-ed in the of-fice.
And I think you'd better hurry up!"
Tommy Dillon came singing up the stairs.
He'd recently joined the choir, so he sang all the time.
I pulled myself away from the window. "Who wants me?" I asked anxiously.
"Mrs. Lip-pett and I think she's mad."
"Oh no!" I groaned.
"What did I do? Were the sandwiches too thick today?
Did a lady visitor see the hole in an orphan's stocking?"
Tommy shrugged. He had no idea, but he followed me downstairs.
The long lower hallway was dark.
One last trustee stood in the open door.
He was a tall man.
He motioned for an automobile to pull up to the door.
As the automobile approached, its headlights cast the man's shadow against the wall.
The shadow had very long arms and legs.
Suddenly my anxiety melted, and I began to laugh.
"That shadow looks just like a giant daddy longlegs!" I whispered to Tommy.
He laughed too.
"Good luck!" he sang as he left me outside Mrs. Lippett's door.
I can find the humor in most things.
So, still smiling about Daddy Longlegs, I knocked on Mrs. Lippett's door.
Much to my surprise, the matron looked almost as cheerful as I did.
"Sit down, Jerusha. I have something to say to you."
I dropped into the nearest chair.
An automobile flashed past the window.
Mrs. Lippett glanced at it.
"Did you notice the gentleman who just left?"
"I only saw his back."
"He's one of our wealthiest trustees.
Over the years he has given large sums of money to the orphanage.
But I'm not allowed to mention his name."
I didn't know what to say.
I wasn't used to talking to her about trustees and their strange requests.
"In the past he has taken an interest in several of our boys.
Do you remember Charles Benton or Henry Freize?
Mr.—I mean, this trustee—sent them both through college.
They repaid him with hard work and success. That's all he required."
The matron glanced at the window again, as if expecting the gentleman to return.
"So far he has only helped boys.
I've never been able to interest him in helping girls.
No matter how smart they were. I guess he dislikes girls." Mrs. Lippett paused.
She seemed to expect a reply here.
So I said the first thing that came into my head. "Yes, ma'am."
Satisfied, Mrs. Lippett continued.
"Today at our meeting, the question of your future came up."
"Yes, ma'am," I replied politely.
Inside I was filled with a mix of curiosity—and dread.
"The question of your future came up at today's meeting," Mrs. Lippett repeated.
"And we discussed it in great detail."
I continued to sit in stunned silence in the matron's office.
"You've done well here, Jerusha," she went on.
"And we let you attend the village high school.
Despite some problems with your behavior."
She frowned at me. I tried to look guilty.
"But you're 18 now and finishing high school.
We can't take care of you for much longer.
As you know, we don't often keep orphans after age 16.
You were lucky to have two extra years here."
I'd worked hard in exchange for my stay at the orphanage for those two extra years.
And my education had always come second.
Today, for example, Mrs. Lippett had kept me home from school to work.
But I was too anxious about my future to say anything.
"Usually we'd send you out to find a job.
However, your grades have been excellent.
Miss Pritchard, who's on our ladies' committee, talked to your English teacher.
The teacher said your work was brilliant.
She also gave Miss Pritchard a story you'd written called 'Blue Wednesday.'"
This time my guilty expression was real.
Mrs. Lippett always said my imagination would get me into trouble.
And now, I guess, it had. "Blue Wednesday" was a work of fiction.
But it was based on the days when the trustees and ladies' committee came to visit.
"Miss Pritchard read that story aloud to us.
I think it was rude to mock the orphanage.
Especially after we've done so much for you." Mrs. Lippett looked at me with disapproval.
"Luckily, some people have a strange sense of humor and found your story funny.
Mr.—that is, the trustee who just left—thought it quite amusing.
On the strength of that disrespectful paper, he's sending you to college!"
"To college?" My eyes grew big.
Mrs. Lippett nodded.
"He waited until after the meeting to discuss the details with me.
They are quite unusual. I must say the gentleman is odd.
He believes you have talent.
He plans to educate you to become a writer!"
"A writer?" I said in shock.
"Who knows if you'll succeed. Only time will tell."
The matron described the trustee's plan.
I would spend the rest of the summer working at the orphanage.
Miss Pritchard would help me choose new clothes.
The trustee would pay for them.
He would also pay my tuition and board directly to the college.
I would also receive an allowance of 35 dollars a month.
"That's a very generous amount, Jerusha," said Mrs. Lippett.
"Far too generous for a girl who has never managed her own money.
But he wanted you to feel equal to the other girls at college."
Mrs. Lippett explained that the trustee's secretary would send me the money every month.
"In return for all this, you must write letters to the trustee," she said.
"These letters should not just be thank-you notes!"
"Then what should I write about?" This gentleman did sound very odd.
"He wants you to write about your studies and your daily life.
Write a letter like you'd write to your parents—if you had parents."
Mrs. Lippett had more strange instructions for me.
The gentleman's name was not Mr. John Smith, yet that was how I should address the letters.
I should mail them to his secretary, Mr. Griggs.
"Mr. Smith will never answer your letters.
He hates writing letters!
However, he wants to keep track of your progress.
He thinks letter writing is good training for a future author.
The letters are the only thanks he requires, so treat them like a bill that must be paid.
If there is an emergency . . ."
"An emergency?" I hadn't thought about having an emergency at college.
"For example, if you are expelled . . . Oh my!
I hope that doesn't happen.
What an embarrassment for the John Grier Home!"
Mrs. Lippett paused for a moment to calm herself, and then began again.
"If you have an emergency, you may write to Mr. Griggs."
I looked at the door.
My head was whirring with excitement, and I wanted to escape.
I needed to think.
I stood up. But Mrs. Lippett shook her head and I sat back down.
"I hope that you're grateful for this wonderful opportunity.
Not many orphans get a chance to rise in the world.
I hope your behavior will make us proud at the John Grier Home.
You must always remember—"
"Yes, ma'am. Thank you, ma'am.
I must sew a patch on one of the orphan's shirts. Right now."
I leaped up and fled, leaving Mrs. Lippett standing there with her mouth open.
September 24
Dear Kind Trustee Who Sends Orphans to College,
Well, here I am at college!
I traveled for four hours on the train.
I never rode on a train before.
College is the biggest, most confusing place I've ever been!
I get lost whenever I leave my room.
It seems strange to write letters to someone I don't know.
Actually, it seems strange to be writing letters at all.
I've only written three or four in my life.
So please forgive me if my letters aren't perfect.
Before I left, Mrs. Lippett and I had a very serious talk.
She told me how to behave for the rest of my life.
Including how I should behave toward you.
"Jerusha, you must be very respectful to the kind gentleman who's doing so much for you," she said.
"But how can I be respectful to someone who wants to be called John Smith?
I wish he'd chosen a more interesting name.
I might as well write letters to Dear Hitching Post."
"Jerusha!" Mrs. Lippett was shocked.
"That is not respectful!"
I thought about you a great deal this summer.
You've taken an interest in me.
That makes me almost feel that I have a family.
It seems as if I belong to somebody now, and I like that feeling.
But when I think about you, I have very little to work with.
I only know three things about you:
1. You are tall.
2. You are rich.
3. You hate girls.
I suppose I could address you as Dear Mr. Girl Hater. But that's rather insulting to me.
Or Dear Mr. Rich Man, but that's insulting to you.
That sounds like money is the only important thing about you.
Besides, maybe you won't stay rich for your whole life.
Lots of wealthy men lose all their money in the stock market.
But at least you'll stay tall all your life!
So I've decided to call you Daddy Longlegs. I hope you won't mind.
It's just a private nickname.
Please don't tell Mrs. Lippett!
Let me tell you about my room, which is in a tower in Fergussen Hall.
It used to be part of the infirmary before the college built the new one.
There are three other girls on the same floor.
There's a senior who wears glasses.
She's always telling us to be quiet.
And two freshmen, Sallie McBride and Julia Rutledge Pendleton.
Sallie has red hair and is quite friendly.
Julia comes from one of wealthiest families in New York.
She hasn't noticed me yet.
Sallie and Julia room together, but the senior and I have singles.
Usually freshmen can't get singles.
But I got one without even asking.
Maybe the college was worried about my behavior around girls raised by proper families.
So there are advantages to being an orphan!
I'm going to enjoy my own room.
Especially after spending 18 years in one room with 20 roommates!
Sallie is the most entertaining person in the world, and Julia is the least entertaining person.
Sallie thinks everything is funny, and Julia is bored with everything.
Julia never makes the slightest effort to be friendly.
She believes that if you're born a Pendleton, you deserve only the best things.
She and I were born to be enemies!
I've fixed up my room with Sallie's help.
She has lived in a real house all her life, so I trusted her advice.
"Let's go to the senior auction," she said the other day.
"The seniors will be selling things they don't want anymore."
When we got to the auction, I had no idea where to begin.
But Sallie steered me toward a wooden desk.
"You should bid on that. It's very nice."
"What about that brown rug over there?" I said.
But when we looked at it, we noticed an ink spot.
"The ink spot will make it less expensive." Sallie looked around.
"And with the money you save, you could buy that wicker chair.
Then you could put the chair over the spot."
So I bought all three items as well as some yellow curtains and cushions.
You can't imagine how fun it is to shop, and get change back after paying!
Especially since I've never had more than a few cents in my life.
I assure you, Daddy dear, I do appreciate the allowance.
Well, it's time for me to end my first letter. One more thing . . .
Sallie just poked her head in my door.
She said, "I'm so homesick that I simply can't stand it. Do you feel that way?"
I smiled a little. "No, I think I'll be all right."
I've never heard of anyone being orphanage sick. Have you?
Yours most respectfully,
Jerusha Abbott
October 10
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Have you ever heard of Michelangelo? I thought I had, but I was wrong.
The other day in English class, the professor said, "Who can tell me something about Michelangelo?"
Just about every girl in the class raised her hand, so I was happy that she called on me.
I spoke up loudly, and everyone could hear me. "He was an angel."
What a mistake! The whole class burst out laughing!
Even the professor was trying to hide a smile.
"Anyone else want to try?" she said.
"Michelangelo was a famous artist who lived in Italy a long time ago," Julia Pendleton said.
"Everybody knows that."
"But he has angel right in the middle of his name!" I thought, blushing furiously.
The trouble with college is that everyone thinks you already know a lot of things.
But I never learned those things in the orphanage.
It's very embarrassing at times.
Now I keep quiet when the girls talk about something I've never heard of.
Then afterward I look it up in the encyclopedia.
You know, Daddy Longlegs, it isn't the work that's hard at college. It's the play.
Half the time I don't know what the girls are talking about.
I'm a stranger in a foreign country, and I don't understand the language.
It's a miserable feeling. But I've had it all my life.
In high school the girls would stand in groups and stare at me.
I was odd and different.
I felt like John Grier Home for Orphans was stamped across my forehead.
There was one nice girl. Sometimes she came over and said something polite.
"How are you today, Jerusha?"
Or "What did you think of the history test, Jerusha?"
Or "I really liked your story when the English teacher read it aloud."
But I hated every one of those high school girls.
And I especially hated the nice one.
I knew she only talked to me because she pitied me.
Nobody here knows that I grew up in an orphanage.
Not even Sallie McBride.
One day when we were walking, Sallie said, "You never talk about your family.
Do you have any brothers or sisters?"
"No, I'm an only child," I quickly replied.
"And I've never heard you mention your parents."
"That's because they're dead."
"Oh, I'm so sorry!" Sallie said.
"I hope I didn't make you feel bad by asking about them."
I shook my head. "No, they've been dead a long time.
I'm only able to go to college because a kind old gentleman is sending me."
That's mostly true, right?
I just want to be like the other girls.
I just want to forget the John Grier Home and get on with my life.
At least Sallie likes me and is my friend.
I've just been reading over this letter.
It sounds pretty unhappy.
But that's probably because I have an essay due tomorrow and a geometry test.
And I have a very sneezy cold.
Oh, I almost forgot! Mrs. Lippett said that you wanted to know everything I'm learning.
Besides English and geometry, I'm taking Latin, French, and biology.
Yesterday the English professor had something nice to say about my latest paper.
"This shows a lot of originality," she said to the whole class.
Which made me feel better about the Michelangelo episode.
The John Grier Home aims to turn out 97 orphans who are all alike.
So it's amazing that I have any originality.
I hope I don't hurt your feelings when I say bad things about the orphanage.
But if I do hurt your feelings, you can stop my allowance.
I guess that's not a polite thing to say.
But you can't expect me to have any manners.
After all, I grew up in an orphanage!
Here's some more news:
I'm trying out for the freshman basketball team.
I'm short, but I'm quick and tough.
While the other girls are jumping, I dodge under their feet and grab the ball.
Practicing is fun!
We're outside in the fall air and the trees are all red and yellow.
Everybody is laughing and shouting.
These are the happiest girls I've ever seen—and I'm the happiest of all.
So there. I've thought of some cheerful things to tell you.
Don't be discouraged when my letters seem sad.
I really love college, and I love you for sending me.
The ten o'clock bell is going to ring in two minutes.
Our day is divided into sections by bells.
We eat and sleep and study by bells.
There goes the bell! Lights out.
Observe how seriously I take the rules here.
The John Grier Home has trained me well.
So I've said nice things about the orphanage too!
Sincerely,
Jerusha Abbott
November 15
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I've changed my name!
I'm still Jerusha to the college.
But I'm Judy to everyone else.
Usually somebody else comes up with a nickname.
(Just like I gave you the name Daddy Longlegs!)
So I guess it's sad that I had to make one up for myself.
But that's not totally true.
One of the little orphans used to call me Judy.
He couldn't say Jerusha when he was learning to talk.
I always wondered where my name came from.
One day, when I still lived at the orphanage, I asked Mrs. Lippett.
"Did my parents name me Jerusha Abbott?"
Mrs. Lippett frowned.
"Oh no. You were like many of the other orphans here.
We didn't know your parents' names or your name.
Someone just left you on the orphanage steps."
"Then where did my name come from?"
"The same place I get all the orphans' names—the telephone book!"
Mrs. Lippett sounded proud of herself.
"You'll find Abbott right there on the first page."
"But where did you find Jerusha?"
"On a tombstone in the cemetery!
Now get back to work, Jerusha, and stop asking questions."
Well, Daddy Longlegs, I never told her this, but I'll tell you.
I've always hated the name Jerusha.
But I like Judy. It's such a silly name.
It belongs to someone who is the complete opposite of me.
A sweet little blue-eyed thing, whose family adores and spoils her.
I may have faults, but no one can say that I've been spoiled.
So from now on, please call me Judy.
I have some more news for you.
I made the basketball team!
You should see the bruise I got the other day at practice.
My left shoulder is blue and purple with orange streaks.
For your information, Julia Pendleton didn't make the team.
Hooray! (I really am very mean sometimes.)
I like college more and more every day.
I like the girls (except for Julia) and the teachers and the classes and the food.
We have ice cream twice a week.
We never have cornmeal mush, which we had often at the orphanage.
Oh, I just remembered something!
I never told you about my clothes.
Before school started, Miss Pritchard took me shopping.
(She's on the ladies' committee at the orphanage, but I guess you remember that.)
Anyway, I thought I'd get one new dress.
Well, maybe two since you were paying for them.
But here's what happened:
"I like this dress for classes," I said as we shopped.
"And I like this one for church. May I get both?"
Miss Pritchard smiled kindly at me.
"You'll need more than two dresses at college."
"I will?"
"Yes, dear. You'll need a suit and an evening dress and at least one dinner dress."
Who knew college required so many clothes?
So, thanks to you, I now own a dress for classes, a dress for church, and a suit.
Plus, two dinner dresses and a silk evening dress!
Can you imagine me—an orphan—in an evening dress?
I also have three pairs of fine white gloves.
At the orphanage I received mittens for Christmas.
But I never had beautiful gloves like these.
I like them so much that I often try them on.
I wish I could wear them to class!
You probably think I'm behaving like a silly girl.
And that you're wasting your money educating me.
But, Daddy Longlegs, if you'd worn blue gingham most of your life, you'd understand!
When I started high school, things got even worse.
My clothes came from the village poor box.
On the first day of school, I sat next to a girl who used to own my dress.
"Did you see her dress?" the girl next to me whispered to a friend.
"Whose dress?"
"The girl from the orphanage. Jerusha."
The second girl studied me.
"Didn't you have a dress like that last year?" she said to the first girl.
"Yes! But it's out of style, so my mother put it in the poor box."
Then they laughed while I turned red with shame.
And this happened every year!
I'll never forget that feeling.
Do you see why I appreciate my new clothes?
Six outfits—all pretty and new and bought just for me.
One last thing: I know I shouldn't expect any letters from you.
And Mrs. Lippett told me not to bother you with questions.
But I just want to know a few things.
Are you very old or just a little old?
Are you completely bald or only a little bald?
It's hard to picture you without some details.
Your well-dressed student,
Judy Abbott
December 19
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
You never answered my question—are you bald?
It's a very important question because I'm trying to draw a picture of you.
While I was drawing last night, Sallie came into my room.
"Who's that?" she asked.
"The kind old man who's sending me to college.
It's difficult to draw him because I've never met him."
"You've never met him, but he's sending you to college?
That's very generous of him."
"Yes, it is."
I didn't look up because I didn't want her to ask any more questions about you—or me.
So I concentrated on drawing your eyes.
I decided to color them gray.
"How do you know what color his eyes are?"
Sallie stood behind me, watching.
"I'm just guessing."
I scribbled in your eyebrows.
They stuck out like a porch roof.
Sallie laughed. "Those are some eyebrows!"
I laughed too. "I think they call them 'beetle brows' in novels."
"I think they do." Sallie laughed again.
But there was no laughter on your face.
For your mouth, I drew a straight line that turned down at the corners.
"He looks like a crabby old thing!" Sallie said.
"Well, maybe he is. He never answers my letters."
"That's rude!" Sallie said.
"He's a kind but rude old man."
Until this point I'd been drawing quickly.
But when I reached the top of your head, I got stuck.
"I can't decide whether he has white or black hair.
Or maybe he has gray hair mixed with dark hair.
What's that called? Oh, I know. Salt and pepper."
"Or maybe he's bald!" Sallie said.
"That's another possibility." I put down my pencil.
"I have to stop drawing until I figure out what kind of hair he has."
"How are you going to find that out?" Sallie asked.
"I'll write him a letter, of course."
So here I am writing you another letter about your hair.
And now, it's not only me who wants to know its color; Sallie wants to know too.
There was something else Sallie wanted to know.
But it was about me, not you.
"Every night you put a Do Not Disturb sign on your door," she said.
"I'm lucky you were free tonight.
What are you so busy doing in here?"
"Oh, just studying."
I rolled up my drawing and tucked it in a desk drawer.
"You must really like to study!" Sallie said.
The truth is, I'm not studying.
I never study at night, no matter how many essays are due the next day.
Instead I just read.
There are so many novels that I've never read, and so many things that I don't know.
The other girls seem to know everything while I have 18 blank years behind me.
I'd never read Oliver Twist or Jane Eyre.
I didn't know that King Henry VIII was married more than once or that Shelley was a poet.
I didn't know that R.L.S. stood for Robert Louis Stevenson or that he wrote Treasure Island.
I'd never seen a picture of the Mona Lisa.
And you probably won't believe this, but I'd never heard of Sherlock Holmes either!
Now I know all these things and a lot more.
But you can see how I needed to catch up. And it's fun!
All day I look forward to the evening.
Then I put on my red bathrobe, sit on my couch, and read.
One book isn't enough.
I usually have four going at once.
Right now I'm reading Little Women.
When I discovered I was the only girl in the dorm who didn't know that book, I said nothing.
I just went and bought it with $1.12 of my allowance.
The Christmas holidays begin next week.
Most of the girls are starting to pack their trunks to go home.
The dormitory hallways are so full of trunks that you can hardly get past them.
Everyone is bubbling over with excitement.
Nobody is studying very much.
I'm going to have a wonderful time, even though I'll be staying here.
There's another freshman who isn't going home.
She's from Texas, so it's too far to travel.
We're planning to take long walks.
And if there's any ice, we want to learn to skate.
Then there's the whole library full of books—and three weeks with nothing to do but read!
Good-bye, Daddy.
I hope that you're feeling as happy as I am.
Yours truly,
Judy
P.S. Don't forget to answer my question.
If you don't want to answer, have your secretary send me a telegram.
He can just say Mr. Smith is quite bald.
Or Mr. Smith is not bald.
Or Mr. Smith has white hair.
And you can deduct the 25 cents for the telegram from my allowance.
Good-bye until January—and have a merry Christmas!
January 10
Dear Daddy Longlegs:
I was so surprised to receive a Christmas gift from you!
I'm not used to getting Christmas presents.
You've already given me so many things. (Actually, everything I own!)
I really don't feel that I deserve anything extra.
But I do like your gift very much.
Do you want to know what I bought with the money?
1. A silver watch to help me get to classes on time
2. A book of poetry
3. A hot-water bottle to put in my bed at night
4. A heavy blanket. My room in the tower is cold!
5. Five hundred sheets of yellow paper. I'm going to start being an author pretty soon
6. A dictionary of synonyms to increase my vocabulary
7. A pair of silk stockings
I don't like to confess that I bought silk stockings.
But you must admit that I tell you everything.
I bought them for a petty reason.
Julia Pendleton often comes into my room to do geometry homework.
And she sits cross-legged on my couch, wearing beautiful silk stockings.
As soon as she returns from vacation, I'll go sit on her couch.
And you know what I'll be wearing—beautiful silk stockings!
So you see what a horrible person I am.
But you already knew I wasn't perfect.
I bet Mrs. Lippett made sure of that!
Meanwhile I'm pretending that my purchases were sent as gifts from my family.
That is, my imaginary family who lives in California.
The watch is from Father; the blanket is from Mother.
My grandmother sent the hot-water bottle.
(She's always worrying that I'll catch a cold in this weather.)
My little brother, Harry, sent the paper.
My sister, Isabel, gave me the stockings, and Aunt Susan wanted me to have the book.
Uncle Harry (little Harry is named after him) sent the dictionary.
He wanted to send chocolates, but I insisted on synonyms.
And now I will tell you what I've done over vacation.
Leonora Fenton is the freshman from Texas who's also staying in the dorm.
I like Leonora, but not as much as I like Sallie McBride.
(Of course, I like you best of all because you're my whole family rolled into one.)
Anyway, Leonora and I have taken long walks nearly every day.
A sophomore named Penelope came too.
One day we walked into town. That's four miles away!
"I'm starving!" I said when we finally reached town.
"So am I! Let's get something to eat," Leonora said.
Penelope pointed across the street.
"Over there is a restaurant where a lot of the college girls like to eat."
We went in and ordered our food.
We had broiled lobster (35 cents).
And for dessert we ate pancakes and maple syrup (15 cents).
Nourishing and cheap!
"Eating in a restaurant is so much fun!" Leonora said.
"Especially for me!" I said.
Then I almost blurted out that I'd grown up in the orphanage.
Instead I made a quick recovery.
"Because whenever I leave campus, I feel like an escaped convict."
"Me too!" Penelope agreed.
"You can't spend all your time in your room. That gets boring."
It's really hard for me not to tell people everything about myself.
If I didn't have you to tell things to, I'd burst!
Here's something else we did over vacation.
On Friday night we made molasses candy.
Several girls from other dorms joined us.
They hadn't gone anywhere for vacation either.
In the large kitchen inside our dorm, the chef wore a white hat and apron.
He handed out hats and aprons to everyone.
"Where did he get so many of these?" I said as I helped Leonora tie her apron.
She shrugged. "Who knows?"
Then we all turned into cooks.
We made a mess, but it was lots of fun.
"Let's take candy to the professors!" one of the older girls said.
So, still wearing our hats and aprons, we paraded through the halls to the faculty parlor.
We interrupted some professors, who were quietly reading.
But we left them sucking on molasses candy, sticky and speechless.
Vacation will be over in two days, and I'll be glad to see all the other girls again.
It's a little lonely with only nine people in a dorm built for four hundred.
I'd be happy except for one thing. Exams are next month!
Yours with love,
Judy
P.S. I hope it's okay to sign my letter that way.
I have to love somebody, and the choice is between you and Mrs. Lippett.
So I choose you!
February 8 (the night before exams)
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
You should see the way the girls in this college are studying!
We've forgotten we ever had a vacation.
I've put so much new information into my brain.
I hope that it stays there until exams are over!
Some girls sell their textbooks when they're done with classes.
But I intend to keep mine.
Then, after I graduate, I'll have my whole education in one bookcase.
If I need a fact, I'll be able to look it up.
So much easier—and more accurate—than trying to remember everything!
Julia Pendleton dropped in this evening.
I thought she'd never leave.
She started talking about family, and I couldn't get her to stop.
"What's your mother's maiden name?" Julia asked me.
"My mother's maiden name?" I said.
I don't even know my mother's name, never mind her name before she was married.
Did you ever hear of asking an orphan such a rude question?
Not that she knows I'm an orphan, of course.
I didn't dare tell her the truth, so I just said the first name that popped into my head.
"She was a Montgomery."
"A Montgomery," Julia repeated.
"Do you mean one of the Boston Montgomerys?
Or was she part of the southern Montgomery family—the ones from Virginia?
Those are the two most prominent branches of the Montgomery family."
I shrugged. "I don't know. She was just a Montgomery."
"Well, my mother is a Rutherford. Her family . . ."
And then she blathered on and on.
I swear her mother's family is so old, they came to the United States on Noah's ark!
And her father's family is connected to all the kings of England.
(Not really, but you know what I mean.
Her family's social status is very important to Julia.
And she cares too much about other people's families too.)
I meant to write you a nice, cheerful letter tonight, but I'm too sleepy—and scared about exams.
The freshman's life is not a happy one.
Your unhappy freshman,
Judy
February 15
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I was so busy studying that I forgot to mail my letter.
So I'll just add to it here.
I have some perfectly dreadful news to tell you.
But I won't begin with that.
I'll try to put you in a good mood first.
I've started my career as an author!
I'm published!
My poem, "From My Tower," is in the February issue of the campus magazine.
I hope you're proud of me!
After all, you're sending me to college to become a writer.
My English professor congratulated me on the way out of chapel this morning.
"Your poem is on the first page," she said.
"That's a great honor for a freshman."
"Thank you, Professor. It's so exciting to see it in print."
"I thought it was a charming piece of writing," she went on.
"The meter in the sixth line is a little off . . . But aside from that, it's quite lovely."
I still like my poem even if the meter is off.
If you care to read it, I'll be glad to send you a copy.
Let's see if I can think of something else pleasant.
Oh, yes! I'm learning to skate and can glide about quite well by myself.
I hardly ever fall down anymore.
I'm doing really well in gym class too.
I've learned how to slide down a rope from the ceiling to the floor.
I can also leap over a bar that is three feet, six inches high.
I soon hope to clear four feet.
We had a very inspiring sermon this morning in chapel.
It was about overlooking the mistakes of others.
And we shouldn't discourage people by judging them harshly.
I really wish you could have heard it.
This is the sunniest winter afternoon.
The sun on the snow is almost blinding.
Icicles are dripping from the fir trees.
All the world is bending under the weight of the snow.
Except for me. I'm bending under the weight of sorrow.
And now for the horrible news.
Are you sure you're in a good mood?
Never mind. I'll try to be brave and just blurt it out.
I failed my Latin and geometry exams.
I'm being tutored in both subjects, and I'll retake both exams next month.
I'm sure to pass next time.
I'm sorry if you're disappointed.
But otherwise, I don't care a bit because I've learned so much on my own.
I've read 17 novels and hundreds of poems.
So you see, I'm actually quite smart!
Will you forgive me this once, if I promise never to fail again?
Regretfully yours,
Judy
March 15
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
It's very stormy outside tonight.
All the girls have turned off their lights and gone to sleep.
But I drank black coffee, so I can't sleep.
I had a party in my room this evening for Sallie and Julia.
We ate sardines, muffins, salad, and fudge.
We also drank coffee, which I'm now regretting!
"I had fun," Julia said as she was leaving.
Imagine that! An orphan successfully entertained a Pendleton.
But Sallie was the true friend.
She stayed and helped with the dishes.
Would you mind pretending that you're my grandmother?
I know that's a strange request!
But tonight the other girls were comparing their grandmothers.
"I have one grandmother," Sallie said.
"She's lots of fun."
"I have two grandmothers," Julia said.
Well, of course, she has more grandmothers than anyone does!
A grandmother seems like a nice relative to have.
When I went into town yesterday, I saw a lace cap trimmed with lilac ribbon.
Would you like that?
I'll buy it for your 83rd birthday, Granny dear.
Meanwhile I am studying verb forms for my Latin exam.
I have studied verb forms for my exam.
I will be studying verb forms for my exam.
The exam is next week, and I have vowed to pass it!
The clock in the chapel is striking midnight.
I feel sleepy after all.
Goodnight, Granny. I love you dearly.
Your granddaughter,
Judy
March 26
Dear Sir:
You never answer any questions.
You never show the slightest interest in anything I do.
You are the most horrible of all the horrible trustees at the orphanage.
You're only educating me out of a sense of duty.
You don't care about me at all!
I don't know a single thing about you.
I don't even know your name.
It's very boring to write to a thing.
I doubt you even read my letters.
I'm sure you toss them into the trash without opening them.
From now on, I will write only about my schoolwork.
I retook my Latin and geometry exams.
I passed them both.
Yours truly,
Jerusha Abbott
April 2
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I am a BEAST.
Please forget that horrible letter I sent last week.
I was feeling lonely and miserable when I wrote.
Plus, I had a sore throat.
I didn't know it, but I was coming down with tonsillitis and the flu.
I'm in the infirmary now.
I've been here for six days!
This is the first time they let me sit up and have pen and paper.
(The head nurse is very bossy!)
I've been thinking about that awful letter the whole time.
I won't get well until you forgive me.
I can't write anything more.
I feel rather shaky; I think I've been sitting up too long.
Please forgive me for being rude and ungrateful.
I was badly brought up.
Yours with love,
Judy
April 4
Dearest Daddy Longlegs,
I am still in the infirmary.
Yesterday afternoon I was sitting in bed, looking at the rain.
I was feeling bored with life in this great institution.
Suddenly a nurse appeared with a long white box.
"For me?" I said in surprise.
"What do you think is in inside?"
The nurse laughed. (She was obviously a nice nurse, not the bossy and mean head nurse.)
"You must have an admirer," she said.
"There's usually only one thing that comes in a box like that—"
"Roses!" I exclaimed as I lifted the cover.
The box was filled with the loveliest pink roses!
Thank you a thousand times, Daddy Longlegs.
Your flowers are the first real present I've ever received.
I know you sent me money for Christmas.
But the roses prove that you were really thinking about me.
And the card is even nicer than the roses.
I can tell you wrote it yourself and didn't have your secretary do it.
I thought the funny handwriting showed lots of personality.
Do you want to know what a baby I am?
I lay down and cried because I was so happy.
I'm sure now that you read my letters.
So I'll make them much more interesting.
I hope you'll keep them tied with a red ribbon and locked in a safe.
But please remove that rude letter and burn it.
I hate to think that you ever read it.
Thank you for thinking of a sick, miserable, and grumpy freshman.
You made me very happy.
You probably have lots of loving family and friends.
So you don't know what it's like to feel alone. But I do.
Good-bye.
I promise never to be rude again because now I know you're a real person.
I also promise never to bother you with any more questions.
Yours forever,
Judy
P.S. Maybe I'll ask just one more question.
Do you still hate girls?
April 20
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Sometimes I worry that I'm not a genius.
This usually happens right after I've read a good book.
Will you be disappointed if I don't become a great author?
In the spring everything is so green and beautiful.
I feel like turning my back on school and playing outside.
It's much more fun to live life than to write about it. I feel—
"Eek!" This letter has been interrupted by someone screaming—me!
Sallie immediately banged on my door. "Are you all right?"
"What's going on?" Julia cried.
"Why are you screaming?"
I opened my door and pointed to a centipede on my chair.
"That's why! It fell from the ceiling and landed next to me!"
Julia took a quick look and shuddered. "Ugh."
Then she went back to her room.
Thank goodness for Sallie, who stayed to help me.
She looked around my room and then grabbed my hairbrush. "Stand back!"
Sallie whacked the centipede with the back of the brush.
(I'll never be able to use that brush again!)
She killed the bug's front end, but its rear fifty feet ran under a chest of drawers.
"It escaped!" Sallie sounded disappointed that we hadn't caught it.
"This dorm is so old and full of centipedes."
"You did your best."
I picked up my cup, which I'd dropped in my rush to escape.
"I hate centipedes!
They're disgusting creatures.
I'd rather find a tiger under my bed!"
The centipede was only one of the annoying things that happened today.
I woke up late because I didn't hear the morning bell.
I broke a shoelace while getting dressed.
I was late for breakfast and my first class.
Then in math class, I had a little argument with the professor.
"I don't understand why my answer is wrong," I said.
"Because you've worked the problem incorrectly," she said.
"But this is how the textbook said to do it!"
I insisted that I was right.
"Look it up again," she said.
"Now, class, let's move on to the next problem."
When I looked in my textbook, I saw she was right. Of course.
On and on went the annoying things.
For lunch we had gray stew.
It reminded me of orphanage food.
In English the professor gave us an impossible poem to analyze.
No one knew what to write.
So we sat there in silence for 45 minutes.
Then it rained, and we couldn't play golf in gym class.
When I got home, my new spring dress had arrived.
But it was so tight that I couldn't sit down.
Oh, and the maid had cleaned my room while I was at classes.
She mixed up all my papers!
Supper was as delicious as lunch.
In other words, more orphanage food.
I was finally sitting down to read when someone knocked on my door.
It was a girl from Latin class.
"May I ask a quick question about the homework?" she said.
She stayed for an hour, talking about the most boring things.
After she left, I decided to write to you.
And that's when the centipede arrived.
So I've had a bad day.
Anybody can face a crisis.
But I think it's harder to deal with life's little annoyances.
That requires spirit.
From now on, I'll try to be that kind of person.
You'll never hear me complain about Julia wearing silk stockings.
Or centipedes dropping in while I'm writing a letter.
Yours truly,
Judy
May 5
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I just received a most disturbing letter from Mrs. Lippett.
She hopes I am behaving myself and doing well in my studies.
(That's not the disturbing part.)
She wants me to return to the orphanage this summer and work there.
(That's the disturbing part.)
I can imagine what happened at this month's meeting of the trustees and ladies' committee.
Mrs. Lippett stood up and said, "Thank you all for coming today.
We must discuss Jerusha Abbott's future."
Then one of the trustees (maybe you?) said, "I thought that was settled.
She's studying to be a writer."
Mrs. Lippett looked very respectful.
"Yes, we did settle that part of her future, sir.
But I'm talking about this summer.
I assume she has no place to go.
She is, of course, an orphan."
Several of the ladies nodded in agreement.
"So I respectfully suggest that Jerusha be allowed to return here," Mrs. Lippett went on.
"There's plenty of work for her to do."
Did anyone speak up to defend me?
Did anyone ask what I thought of this idea?
Obviously not.
So I'll tell you what I think of Mrs. Lippett's proposal.
I HATE THE JOHN GRIER HOME.
I would rather die than go back there!
Even for just a summer.
Yours most truthfully,
Jerusha Abbott
May 27
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
The campus looks especially beautiful right now.
The trees and the grass are green.
The flowers are blooming.
And all the girls are wearing their spring dresses.
Everyone is happy because vacation is coming.
(For the moment we're pretending that exams aren't coming too.)
I wish I could show you the campus.
I'm quite good at giving tours.
In fact I just gave one to a man.
And not just any man.
A quite charming man—Julia's uncle, Mr. Jervis Pendleton.
He's her father's younger brother, but she doesn't know him very well.
It seems he glanced at her as a baby and decided he didn't like her.
He hasn't paid much attention to her since.
But yesterday Uncle Jervis was in town on business.
So he decided to come here and visit his niece.
When he arrived, Julia was in a panic.
She came running into my room.
"Judy, you have to help me!
My uncle just showed up!
He's downstairs waiting for me.
But I have a class in ten minutes.
And so does Sallie.
Could you walk him around the campus until I get back?"
"Um . . ." I really didn't want to do this because I don't care much for Pendletons.
"Oh, please," Julia begged me.
"You only have to do it this one time.
How hard can it be to talk to a man for an hour?"
"All right." I sighed.
"I'll try to keep him amused, but hurry back."
We went downstairs, and there he was, sitting very properly on a sofa.
His hat and gloves were beside him.
So was his walking stick.
He grabbed them and popped up as soon as Julia and I arrived.
"This is Judy Abbott," Julia said, introducing us.
"She'll show you around campus until my class is over."
I didn't know what to talk about, but Uncle Jervis turned out to be the nicest man.
He's a real human being—not like a Pendleton at all.
We had a lovely time, and now I'm longing for an uncle.
Would you mind pretending you're my uncle instead of my grandmother?
We walked all over campus, from the dorms to the athletic grounds.
I pointed out the library, the classrooms, and the new infirmary.
"This a wonderful tour, Miss Abbott.
But I'm wondering if we might have some tea.
How about going to the College Inn?"
"Oh, I don't know." I was worried about Julia.
"Shouldn't we ask Julia to join us?
And maybe Sallie too?
I'm sure they're finished with class by now."
I glanced at my watch.
He shook his head.
"I don't like my niece to drink too much tea.
It makes her nervous."
"Oh, I see. Well, then I guess it would be all right."
We walked to the inn, which is right off campus.
I realize I don't know you very well, Daddy Longlegs.
But something about Uncle Jervis reminded me of a younger version of you.
It's probably because he's so tall.
At the inn we sat at a lovely table on the balcony.
I thought we would just have tea, but Uncle Jervis was hungry.
"Oh, no, Miss Abbott. We must have something to eat."
So we had muffins and marmalade, plus ice cream and cake!
I was so full; I knew I wouldn't have room for supper.
Uncle Jervis makes you feel like you've known him forever.
We had the best time together.
"There weren't many people at the inn today," he said as we left.
I laughed. "It's the end of the month.
The girls have spent most of their allowances."
"Well, I'm glad we went.
Now what time is it?"
It was his turn to look at his watch.
"I have to run for my train!"
"But you must see Julia!" I said.
We hurried back to the dorm, and he briefly spoke to Julia.
After he left, she was furious with me for taking him to tea.
"But he insisted!" I said.
"You should have said no.
He was my guest, not yours.
I wanted to take him to tea."
I felt quite bad about it until this morning.
That's when three boxes of chocolate arrived for Julia, Sallie, and me.
Julia has forgiven her uncle.
Meanwhile I can't believe that a man sent me candy.
I feel like a regular girl instead of an orphan.
And another nice thing just happened.
I received a letter from your secretary.
He said you want me to spend the summer on a farm.
He'll send the details soon.
Hooray! I won't have to spend the summer washing dishes at the orphanage. Thank you!
I wish you would come for tea someday.
I'm sure I'd like you.
Your niece,
Judy
June 10
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I just got here, but already Lock Willow Farm seems like heaven to me!
Mr. and Mrs. Semple are so kind.
The farmhouse is more than a hundred years old with a lovely porch out front.
My room has two big windows, and there's even a table where I can write.
I'm going to write a novel this summer.
I can't believe that I get to spend three months here in Connecticut.
You've given me more than I deserve.
You should hear the frogs croaking and the pigs squealing!
I can't wait until tomorrow to explore.
It's only half past eight, but I have to try to sleep.
We rise at five in the morning on the farm.
Good night,
Judy
July 15
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
How did your secretary know about Lock Willow Farm?
I'm curious because I've just learned something interesting.
Mr. Jervis Pendleton used to own this farm!
He gave it to Mrs. Semple, who had been his nanny.
Did you ever hear such a coincidence?
Mrs. Semple still calls him "Master Jervie."
She's always talking about what a sweet little boy he was.
She even has one of his baby curls saved in a box.
(He had red hair!)
Mrs. Semple was very impressed that I'd met him.
She thinks Master Jervie is the best member of the Pendleton family.
And so do I!
The farm gets more entertaining every day.
I rode on a hay wagon yesterday.
We have three big pigs and nine little piglets.
They all have huge appetites!
There are also lots of chickens, ducks, and turkeys.
Every day my job is to collect the eggs.
Yesterday I fell off a beam in the barn loft.
When I came into the kitchen, I showed Mrs. Semple my scraped knee.
"Oh, dear, let me clean that for you."
She rubbed my knee with a liquid that stung.
"Ouch!" I cried.
"How did you scrape your knee?" she asked.
"The black hen made her nest on a beam in the barn loft.
I fell when I was trying to get the eggs.
Why would she build her nest up there?"
"To keep her eggs safe." Mrs. Semple laughed.
"It seems only yesterday that Master Jervie fell off the very same beam.
And I believe he scraped that very same knee."
We have six calves and I've chosen names for most of them.
One is named Sallie, and another is Judy.
There's also a dull, ordinary one that I called Julia.
I hope you don't mind, but I've also named one Daddy Longlegs.
It has a very sweet personality.
July 16
I meant to finish this letter yesterday.
But then I remembered that I'd promised to pick blackberries for supper.
So I went off and left the letter on the table.
What do you think I found today?
A real daddy longlegs, sitting in the middle of the page!
I gently set it on the windowsill so it could escape.
I'd never hurt one of them.
They always remind me of you!
When I finish this letter, I'm going to read a book that I found in the attic.
It belonged to Jervis Pendleton.
I know this because he wrote his name on the first page.
I showed it to Mrs. Semple last night.
We were sitting on the front porch after supper.
"Oh, I remember this book."
She took it from my hand and smiled fondly.
"Master Jervie read it over and over.
He spent the whole summer here one year after he'd been ill."
"How old was he?"
"Hmm." Mrs. Semple stopped to think.
"He must have been 11 that year.
He was always running up the stairs, making an awful racket.
I always had to remind him to close the screen door, so the bugs would stay out.
And, of course, he was constantly asking for cookies."
"I'm sure you always gave him cookies," I said.
"Well, yes." Mrs. Semple smiled at the memory.
"But not before meals, of course."
She handed the book back to me.
I know Master Jervie enjoyed this book because his fingerprints are all over the pages!
Mrs. Semple talks about him all the time.
Now I think of him as a nice but dirty little boy full of adventure.
She says he was a brave and truthful child.
Here at the farm, I can't think of him as that grown man with a silk hat and walking stick.
His toys are still in a corner of the attic!
I'm sorry that he's a Pendleton because he's clearly much better than that other Pendleton I know.
I haven't had time to begin my novel.
But I've learned how to make doughnuts!
Your affectionate orphan,
Judy
September 20
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Here I am—a sophomore!
I was sorry to leave Lock Willow, but glad to see the campus again.
Before I left the farm, I weighed myself on the flour scales at the general store.
I gained nine pounds over the summer!
I highly recommend Lock Willow Farm as a health resort.
It's so nice to come back to a familiar place.
I'm beginning to feel at home at college.
In fact, I'm starting to feel at home in the world.
And now, Daddy Longlegs, listen to this.
Who do you think my roommates are?
Sallie McBride and Julia Rutledge Pendleton.
Seriously, that's the truth.
We have three bedrooms and a study.
Last spring Sallie and I decided to room together.
Julia wanted to stay with Sallie.
I can't imagine why.
They're not the least bit alike.
But I guess Pendletons don't like change.
Anyway, here we are.
Jerusha Abbott, formerly of the John Grier Home for Orphans, is now rooming with a Pendleton.
Can you imagine that?
This semester I'm starting chemistry, a very strange subject.
I'm also taking world history, Shakespeare, and French.
There's one girl in my French class, who chatters away in French.
Her family lived in France for three years, so she went to school there.
She's far ahead of the rest of us in class.
I had such poor French training in high school.
I wish my parents had dropped me off at a French school instead of at the orphanage.
On second thought, forget about that.
If I'd gone to school in France, I wouldn't know you!
And I would rather know you than French.
Yours,
Judy
P.S. Sallie is running for class president.
Julia and I are helping her campaign.
October 17
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I have to tell you about the strange things we talk about at supper here.
The other night we had lemon gelatin for dessert.
That led to the following discussion:
"Suppose we filled the college swimming pool with lemon gelatin," Sallie said.
"You'd get in trouble!" Julia said.
"Wait! I'm not finished.
Could a person swim on top of it, or would she sink?"
"How could you swim through lemon gelatin?" I licked my spoon.
"I'm sure the best swimmer in the world would sink."
"I think I could swim in it," said Sallie.
We debated the question for half an hour and still couldn't agree.
"It would be very strange to drown in gelatin," said Julia.
"Whether lemon or a different flavor.
But I have another question.
What shape are the rooms in an octagon house?"
"They're square," said Sallie.
Quite a few of the other girls agreed with her.
I tried to remember last year's geometry class.
"No, I think the rooms would be shaped like a piece of pie."
That led to another round of discussion at our table.
We still couldn't agree, but I'm sure I'm right.
What do you think, Daddy Longlegs?
Finally, I had a question for the group.
Suppose you were sitting inside a hollow sphere made of mirrors.
Where would it stop reflecting your face and start reflecting your back?
No one spoke because no one had an answer.
Julia shook her head.
"The more you think about that one, the more puzzling it gets."
So you see what deep discussions we have over supper!
Did I ever tell you the results of the election? Sallie won!
As her roommates, Julia and I are very important people now on campus.
But it can be a strain living with a president!
Best,
Judy
November 12
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
We beat the freshmen at basketball yesterday!
Now we'd really like to beat the juniors.
Sallie has invited me to spend Christmas vacation with her family.
I couldn't believe she asked me.
We were walking back to our room after classes.
"I'd love to go!" I gave her a hug.
"That's so nice of you to invite me."
"You'll like my family," she said.
"I have a sister and two brothers, and my grandmother lives with us too.
Oh, and we have a cat. You like cats, right?"
"Sure!"
I was so happy that I practically skipped the rest of the way to our dorm.
I've never stayed in a real house with a real family.
I mean, the farmhouse at Lock Willow was a real house.
But Mr. and Mrs. Semple were old, and there weren't any children around.
Packing my trunk and going away is much more fun than staying here for vacation.
I'm so excited!
And now I must run to rehearsal.
I'm in the Thanksgiving show, but you'd never recognize me.
I wear a velvet tunic and a blond wig because I'm a prince!
Yours,
Judy
December 31
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I meant to thank you for your Christmas check before today.
But life in the McBride house is very busy!
I used the money for a new evening gown.
I must confess that I didn't need a new gown.
I just wanted one!
I've been having the most wonderful vacation.
Sallie lives in a big, old-fashioned brick house.
It's the kind of house I used to imagine when I lived at the orphanage.
I never imagined that I'd step inside such a place.
But here I am!
I think Sallie is surprised at how much I like her house.
On our first day here, she showed me around, and I couldn't stop talking.
"There are so many rooms!" I said.
"I'll probably get lost."
"We did lose my little brother, Tom, one rainy day.
We were playing hide-and-seek and couldn't find him.
We finally gave up and went downstairs.
Half an hour later, he came sliding down the banister in the front hall!"
"You have so many fireplaces!"
I said as we stepped into one of the parlors.
Sallie laughed. "We'll make popcorn over the fire one night.
Speaking of food, let's go visit the kitchen.
We should say hello to Mrs. Jamison, the cook."
We stepped into a great big sunny kitchen.
Mrs. Jamison, a large, cheerful woman, was busy making pies.
She stopped to give Sallie a hug.
"I saved you a piece of dough to bake."
The cook pointed to a miniature pie plate.
"Let's sprinkle it with cinnamon sugar," Sallie said to me.
"That'll make it taste even better."
Sallie put the dough in the oven, and in a few minutes, we were eating a wonderful treat!
All the meals here are delicious, and we have such fun at the table.
Everybody laughs and jokes and talks at once.
Besides Sallie's parents, her grandmother and siblings live here.
Sallie's sister, Ellen, is only three, and she's the sweetest little thing.
Sallie's younger brother, Tom, is always getting scolded, but in a loving way.
He never remembers to wipe his feet when he enters the house.
He reminds me of Master Jervie!
Sallie also has a handsome big brother named Jimmy.
He's a year older than we are, and he's a junior at Princeton.
We've done so many things since I arrived.
I can't even begin to tell you about them all.
Mr. McBride owns a factory.
On Christmas Eve he had a Christmas party for his employees' children.
There was a Christmas tree, and one of the rooms in the factory was decorated with evergreens and holly.
Jimmy was dressed as Santa Claus.
He wore a white beard and a red suit.
A pillow at his waist made him jolly and plump.
"You're looking rather fat, brother dear," Sallie said.
"Shh!" I poked her arm.
"Don't let the children hear you.
Let them think he's the real Santa Claus!"
"This young lady is perfectly correct," Jimmy said to Sallie.
"I don't know who you're calling brother dear." Then he turned to me.
"I hope you've been a good girl this year.
What would you like for Christmas?"
I laughed.
He's so much fun.
Sallie and I helped him hand out the presents.
It was a strange sensation to be handing out gifts.
The whole scene reminded me of Christmas at the orphanage.
Only this time I was playing the part of a kindly trustee instead of an orphan.
I even kissed one sticky little boy.
But I didn't pat anyone on the head.
I used to hate being patted on the head!
Right after Christmas the McBrides had a dance at their house—for me!
"This is the first real ball I've ever attended," I said nervously to Sallie.
She was helping me get dressed.
"Well, you look beautiful!" she said.
"Turn around so I can see the back of your dress."
I was wearing my new evening gown.
(Your Christmas present. Many thanks for that!)
Plus white satin slippers and long white gloves.
Sallie had to button the gloves for me.
It's hard to do that by yourself.
"You look perfect," Sallie said. "Jimmy will be very impressed."
And indeed he was.
"You look lovely," he said to me.
And then we danced every dance.
That is, until his mother said he must be polite and ask someone else.
I was utterly, totally, completely happy that night.
I only wished that Mrs. Lippett could have seen me dancing with Jimmy McBride.
Please tell her about it the next time you visit the John Grier Home.
Happy New Year,
Judy
P.S. Would you be disappointed if I didn't turn out to be a great author?
What if I'm just a regular girl who likes wearing pretty clothes and dancing with good-looking boys?
January 17
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Today is a very rainy day!
I like winter to act like winter with snow, not rain.
I still managed to have a good day because Julia's uncle came to visit again.
This time he brought a five-pound box of chocolates!
There are advantages to being Julia's roommate.
We had to ask permission to entertain him.
It's a good thing the dean didn't see Uncle Jervie.
If she knew how young and handsome he is, she'd never let him set foot in our study!
The three of us seemed to amuse Uncle Jervie.
In fact, he decided to catch a later train, so he could have tea with us.
I started to make cheese sandwiches on brown bread.
"Let me help you," Uncle Jervie said.
I handed him a knife, and he sliced the cheese.
Then we sat around eating sandwiches and drinking tea.
"I spent last summer at Lock Willow Farm," I said, passing him a cup of tea.
"Did you? I have many happy memories of that place."
We had a wonderful time gossiping about the Semples and all the farm animals.
"Mrs. Semple seems awfully fond of you, Master Jervie," I said.
He smiled when I called him Master Jervie, but he didn't seem to mind.
"And I'm very fond of her.
The last time I was there, the Semples had a new colt.
Now what was its name?"
He took a bite of sandwich.
"Oh, I remember. Grover."
I laughed. "You haven't been there for ages then!
Grover is so old that he can barely limp around the pasture."
"Well, it was a long time ago.
Does Mrs. Semple still keep doughnuts on the bottom shelf of the pantry?"
"Yes! In a yellow pot with a blue plate on top."
"That's how she stored them when I was a child.
Let's see what else I remember."
He took a sip of tea.
"Is there still a groundhog hole under the pile of rocks in the far pasture?"
I nodded. "And there are still groundhogs living there!
They must be the great-great-great-great-great-great grandchildren of the ones you used to see."
So we chatted like that for the rest of teatime.
He talked mostly to me, leaving Julia and Sallie to talk to each other.
After he left, Julia said, "I've never seen my uncle in such a good mood.
He's usually so aloof that I'm afraid to approach him."
I think that's partly Julia's fault.
She doesn't know how to talk to men.
By the way, Uncle Jervie ate four cheese sandwiches.
Yours truly,
Judy
February 4
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Jimmy McBride sent me a huge Princeton banner.
My roommates are not happy about it.
"I'm very glad he remembered me," I said, unfolding the banner.
"But I don't know what to do with it.
Look at the size of this thing!
It's as big as one end of our study."
"Well, you're not hanging it in here," Sallie said.
"It really clashes with our decor," Julia said.
I had to agree with that.
Can you imagine if I added a giant orange and black banner?
"But it's such nice, warm, thick felt."
I patted the banner.
"I hate to waste it."
"You're not hanging it in here," Sallie repeated firmly.
So now I have to figure out what to do.
Do you think it's improper to have Jimmy's banner made into a bathrobe?
My old one shrank in the wash.
I realize I haven't mentioned my studies.
Sometimes it's confusing to study five different subjects at once.
"The mark of a true scientist is a passion for detail," my chemistry professor says.
"Don't keep your eyes glued to the details," my history professor says.
"You must look at the broader view."
I hope I can remember which one wants what.
Exams are next week, but who's afraid?
Your student,
Judy
March 5
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I never told you about exams.
I passed everything. Phew!
I know the secrets of studying now, so I'm never going to fail again.
This week I'm reading Hamlet for my Shakespeare class, which continues this semester.
It's WONDERFUL!
Lying in bed at night, I pretend I'm Ophelia.
But I change some things in the play.
I keep Hamlet amused all the time and make him dress warmly.
As a result, he's a happy fellow.
We're ruling Denmark.
The kingdom is running beautifully.
Hamlet governs while I'm in charge of the charities.
I've just built some first-class orphanages.
Let me know if you and the other trustees want to visit.
I'm sure you'll pick up some useful ideas for the John Grier Home.
Yours most graciously,
OPHELIA, Queen of Denmark
March 28
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
So many good things have happened!
I won the short story contest that the college magazine holds every year.
And I'm just a sophomore!
The other contestants were mostly seniors.
When I saw my name posted, I couldn't believe I'd won.
First prize is twenty-five dollars.
I also got a part in the spring play, As You Like It.
That's something else that Shakespeare wrote.
Besides Hamlet, of course.
Last but not least . . . Julia, Sallie, and I are traveling to New York City next weekend.
We're going to do some spring shopping.
Master Jervie has invited us to the theater on Saturday.
Julia will stay at home with her family.
But Sallie and I are going to stay at a hotel.
I've never been in a hotel or a theater!
And what do you think we're going to see at the theater?
Hamlet. Imagine that!
We studied it for a month in Shakespeare class.
I know it by heart.
I'm so excited that I can hardly sleep.
Yours,
Judy
April 7
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
My goodness! New York City is big!
Do you really live in all that confusion?
It'll take me months to recover from just two days there.
I can't begin to tell you everything I saw.
But I guess you know what New York is like.
Sallie, Julia, and I went shopping on Saturday morning.
Those shop windows were filled with so many lovely things.
They make you want to devote your life to clothes.
"I need some new hats," Julia said.
We entered the most gorgeous shop on the block.
The walls were white and gold.
There were blue silk curtains and gold chairs.
A pretty blond woman in a black gown welcomed us.
It was like paying a social call at someone's home!
"Please take a seat in front of the mirror," she said to Julia.
Then the woman brought over a selection of beautiful hats.
"Each one is lovelier than the last," Sallie said.
I could only nod and watch as Julia tried them on.
At last Julia pointed to the two loveliest hats of all.
"I'll take both of those."
She handed the woman a card with her name and address.
"Please send them to this address."
"Julia never asked the prices!" Sallie whispered to me.
"I know!" I whispered back.
"I cannot imagine being able to buy any hat I wanted!"
Next we met Master Jervie for lunch at Sherry's.
Have you ever been there?
Picture Sherry's—it's a really fancy restaurant.
Then picture the dining room at the orphanage with its plain white dishes and worn-out tables.
Quite the contrast!
I ate my fish with the wrong fork.
But the waiter very kindly gave me another one.
I don't think anyone noticed.
After lunch we went straight to the theater.
I sat between Sallie and Master Jervie.
"Are you eager to see the play?" he asked me.
"Oh yes! I've been looking forward to it!"
I was so excited, and the play hadn't even started yet.
Hamlet was amazing! Dazzling! Marvelous!
"Isn't Shakespeare wonderful?" Master Jervie said to me at intermission.
"I thought I liked Hamlet while I was reading it, but now . . .
It's so much better onstage than reading it at school."
Master Jervie smiled.
I'm sure my eyes were wide as saucers.
But I don't care.
Maybe I'll become an actress instead of a writer.
I'll send you tickets for all my shows.
Then I'll smile at you from the stage.
Please wear a red rose in your buttonhole.
I'd hate to smile at the wrong man.
We returned to school on Saturday night.
We ate supper on the train. There were little tables with pink lamps.
"I never heard of meals being served on a train," I said as we sat down.
"Where on earth did you grow up?" Julia asked.
"In a village," I said quietly.
I hoped she wouldn't ask any more questions.
"Did you ever travel?" she asked.
"Not till I went to college.
And then it was only 160 miles, and we didn't eat in the dining car."
She smiled. "I can't imagine that.
You say the funniest things!"
I try not to say funny things, but they pop out when I'm surprised.
At least I don't make as many mistakes as I used to.
I'm learning how people who didn't grow up in orphanages live.
So I feel more comfortable around the other girls now.
I forgot to tell you about our flowers!
Master Jervie gave us each a bunch of violets and lilies of the valley.
Wasn't that sweet of him?
I never used to care much for men.
But I'm changing my mind.
Yours always,
Judy
April 10
Dear Mr. Rich Man,
Here's your check for fifty dollars.
Thank you very much, but I can't keep it.
I'm sorry I wrote all that silly stuff about the hat shop.
It was just that I'd never seen anything like it.
I wasn't hinting that you should buy me hats!
And I was definitely not begging!
My allowance is generous enough that I can buy all the hats I need.
I don't want to take any more money from you than I have to.
Sincerely yours,
Jerusha Abbott
April 11
Dearest Daddy Longlegs,
Will you please forgive me for yesterday's letter?
After I mailed it, I went to the post office and tried to get it back.
I waited in line forever.
Finally it was my turn.
"I mailed a letter and now I need it back," I said to the clerk.
I tapped my fingers impatiently on the counter.
"I can't do that, miss," he said.
"It's against the rules."
"But I only mailed it an hour ago!
Surely it hasn't left the post office.
Can't you see if it's still here? Please!"
"It's against the rules," he repeated.
"Once a letter has been mailed, the post office can't return it to the sender.
You'll have to write him again. Next!"
The clerk motioned to the person behind me in line.
"How do you know it was addressed to a man?" I asked.
"This is a college town full of young ladies.
These things happen all the time."
The clerk sneered at me.
"A young lady writes something in anger to her young man, and then has second thoughts.
Just write him another letter today.
I'm sure your young man will understand."
"But . . . but . . ." I was so angry I could hardly speak.
I turned to go, but then I thought of something to say.
"He's not a young man!"
Both the clerk and the lady behind me looked shocked as I stormed out of the post office.
Now it's the middle of the night.
I'm sitting in bed, writing on paper torn from my history notebook.
I've been awake for hours thinking about what a horrible person I am.
I'm truly sorry that I returned your check with such a rude letter.
You're very kind to take so much trouble over a silly hat.
But I really can't accept your check.
You see, I'm different from other girls.
They can accept money from other people.
They have aunts and uncles and grandparents.
But I have no one.
Yes, I like to pretend you're part of my family, but really I'm alone in this world.
Sometimes that idea fills me with so much fear that I can hardly breathe.
So I try not to think about it.
I can't accept any more money than necessary because I want to pay you back.
Even if I become a famous author, I won't be able to repay a huge debt.
I love pretty hats and things, but I must not go into debt for them.
Do you understand?
Please forgive me for being so rude.
I have an awful habit of writing letters when I'm upset.
I should stop and think before I mail them.
If I sometimes seem thoughtless and ungrateful, I never mean it.
In my heart I thank you for the life and independence you've given me.
My childhood was just one long stretch of boredom, and now I'm so happy every moment.
I can't believe it's true.
I feel like a heroine in a novel.
Speaking of novels . . . I've been reading Jane Eyre.
Did you know that Jane was an orphan?
The other day I was reading about her troubles at the orphanage.
I got so angry that I had to take a walk!
I understood exactly how she felt.
I'm not saying that the John Grier Home was like poor Jane's orphanage.
We had plenty to eat and warm clothes to wear.
But there was one similarity: Our lives were boring and uneventful.
Nothing nice ever happened, except we got ice cream on Sundays.
And even that was predictable because it happened every Sunday.
We never had any adventures.
Everybody likes a few surprises in life; that's a normal thing to want.
Before I fall asleep at night, I like to imagine the perfect orphanage.
I plan out the smallest details: the meals, the clothes, the lessons, the entertainment.
I even imagine the punishments because I'm sure some of my orphans will be naughty.
But I'll make sure all the orphans are happy.
Everybody should have a happy childhood to look back on.
I didn't have a happy childhood, but I'm very happy now, thanks to you.
Love always,
Judy
May 4
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
The college had a Field Day last Saturday.
First, the classes paraded across the campus.
All the girls wore white dresses.
Our class—the sophomores—carried red balloons.
They looked very festive when they got loose and floated away!
Sallie and I weren't in the parade because we were competing.
We each won an event!
Sallie won the pole vault, and I won the fifty-yard dash.
Between events, about a dozen clowns entertained the spectators.
Julia dressed up as an old gentleman with a long coat and whiskers.
She made everyone laugh.
I never dreamed that a Pendleton could be so funny.
(I hope that doesn't offend Jervie. I don't consider him a true Pendleton anyway.)
I haven't mentioned my classes lately, but we're still having them every day.
It's a relief though, to stop studying and discuss life with you.
Not that you ever respond!
But that's your own fault.
You're welcome to reply to my letters anytime.
Good night,
Judy
June 2
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
The nicest thing has happened.
The McBrides have asked me to spend the summer at their house in the Adirondack Mountains!
I just received a letter from Mrs. McBride inviting me.
"You really must come!
We'll have so much fun!" Sallie said, when I showed her the letter.
"Our summer house is on a lovely little lake in the middle of the woods.
And you'll never guess what the house is made of."
I laughed. "I won't even try."
"Logs! All the houses in that area are made of logs."
I didn't want to admit that I'd never been to a summer house—never mind a log house.
Instead I asked, "What's there to do?"
"Oh, lots of things!" Sallie's eyes sparkled with delight.
"We go canoeing on the lake and take long walks on the trails to the other houses.
Our neighbors are so friendly, it's as if we're all in a club.
There's even a clubhouse, where we have dances once a week."
"Dances!" I said.
"That sounds like fun, but who will we dance with?"
"Don't worry about that.
My brother Jimmy is having a college friend visit for part of the summer.
So we'll have plenty of men to dance with."
"That does sound like fun," I said.
"It's so nice of your mother to ask me."
"She really liked you when you visited us at Christmas.
Oh, Judy, say that you'll come!"
"Of course I will!" I gave her a hug.
So, Daddy Longlegs, this isn't much of a letter.
I just wanted you to know that I'm busy this summer.
And I'm also very happy!
Yours,
Judy
June 5
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Your secretary has written that you want me to decline Mrs. McBride's invitation.
Instead you want me to spend the summer at Lock Willow Farm.
Why, why, WHY?
You don't understand at all.
Mrs. McBride really does want me to come.
I won't be the least bit of trouble.
In fact, I can probably help out.
The McBrides won't be bringing many servants, and Sallie and I can do lots of useful things.
It'll be a good chance for me to learn about housekeeping.
Every woman ought to know how to keep house, and I only know orphanage-keeping.
Besides, there aren't any girls our age at the lake, so Mrs. McBride wants me to stay as a friend for Sallie.
We're planning to read all our books for next year's sociology class.
The professor said it would be helpful if we finished our reading over the summer.
I know I'll remember things better if Sallie and I read the books together and then discuss them.
Just to live in the same house as Mrs. McBride will be educational.
She's the most interesting and charming woman in the world.
She knows everything!
Think of how many summers I've spent with Mrs. Lippett and how I'll appreciate the contrast.
You don't have to worry that I'll take up too much room.
When the McBrides have a lot of company, they pitch tents in the woods.
Then all the boys sleep out there.
It's going to be such a nice, healthy summer.
We'll be exercising outside almost every day.
Jimmy McBride is going to teach me to ride a horse and paddle a canoe.
It will be the fun, carefree vacation that I've never had.
I think every girl deserves that at least once in her life.
Of course, I'll follow whatever instructions you give me.
But please, PLEASE let me go.
I've never wanted anything so much.
Yours,
Judy
June 9
Dear Mr. Smith,
Your secretary has sent me your instructions.
I leave on Friday to spend the summer at Lock Willow Farm.
Sincerely,
Miss Jerusha Abbott
August 3
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Almost two months have passed since I last wrote to you.
That wasn't nice of me, but I haven't liked you very much this summer.
(I'm just being honest!)
I was so disappointed about not going to the McBrides' summerhouse.
I don't understand why you wouldn't let me go.
Here's how I wish our conversation had gone:
Judy: "Please, sir, may I go to Sallie's house for the summer?
It will be the best summer of my life."
Daddy Longlegs: "Of course, my dear. Go have a good time.
Meet lots of new people and learn lots of new things.
Live outside in the fresh air.
Rest and grow strong, so you'll be ready for another year of hard work."
But we didn't have a conversation.
You didn't even write me a letter.
I only received a line from your secretary, ordering me to Lock Willow Farm.
I hate how impersonal your commands are.
That's what hurts my feelings.
I'd like to receive a handwritten message from you.
But instead I get those cold typewritten notes from your secretary.
If you ever acted like you cared, I'd do anything for you.
I know we had a deal.
You promised to pay for my education.
In return, I was to write nice long letters without expecting any response from you.
You're keeping your promise.
And I suppose you think I'm not keeping mine.
But it's a hard bargain, Daddy Longlegs. It really is.
I'm so lonely.
When I was sick last year, you sent me a handwritten note.
Now, when I'm feeling forgotten, I often reread your card.
You're the only person I have to care about.
And I really don't know anything about you.
Here's what I truly want to say:
Although my feelings are still hurt, I've decided to forgive you for sending me to the farm.
But I still don't enjoy getting Sallie's letters about the fun they're having!
So let's begin again.
I've been writing and writing this summer.
I've finished four short stories and sent them to four different magazines.
I have a desk in the corner of the attic where Jervie used to play on rainy days.
Speaking of rain . . . it rained here for a week.
But now the air is fresh and the sun is shining.
If you're stuck in that hot, crowded New York City, I'd like to send you this bright, lovely day.
Good afternoon,
Judy
August 10
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
You'll never guess who's coming to Lock Willow!
Jervis Pendleton!
The mail is delivered once a day around noon.
Mrs. Semple opened his letter right after lunch today.
We were still sitting at the table.
"Oh my! Jervie wants to visit us!" she exclaimed.
"He hasn't been here for years."
"So why is he coming now?" I asked.
"He says he's tired and needs a break.
He wants to rest on a nice, quiet farm."
"How long is he staying?"
Mrs. Semple read the letter again.
"He doesn't say.
Maybe he'll stay for a week or maybe two or three.
He'll see how he feels when he gets here.
But, oh my! We have so much cleaning to do before he arrives!"
I glanced around the dining room and didn't see a speck of dirt.
"What is there to clean?"
"The whole house!
We must clean it from top to bottom and wash all the curtains.
I hope our neighbor is available.
I want to hire her to wash the windows.
And you must go into town for me this afternoon, Judy.
We'll need two cans of brown paint for the stairs and back hall floor."
I couldn't believe the change that had come over Mrs. Semple.
She seemed almost frantic as she started a list for me.
"How long do we have to do all this?" I asked.
Mrs. Semple looked at the letter again and shook her head.
"I have no idea.
He doesn't say if he's arriving today—or in two weeks."
August 11
I didn't get this letter mailed because I was so busy helping Mrs. Semple.
There was no sign of Jervie yesterday.
The house is now immaculate.
I hope he arrives soon.
