Otherwise we'll have to clean all over again.
I'm looking forward to having someone to talk to besides Mrs. Semple.
She's nice, but she can be rather boring.
All she ever talks about is what happens right here on the farm.
I suppose I was like that at the orphanage.
But at college I got used to having real conversations about a variety of things.
So I'll be glad to see Jervie.
I'll tell you all about his visit in my next letter.
Yours always,
Judy
August 25
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Well, Jervie is here, and we're having such a nice time!
At least I am, and I hope he is too.
He has been here ten days and doesn't show any signs of leaving.
The way Mrs. Semple spoils him is awful!
I don't understand how he turned out to be such a nice person.
He and I eat at a little table set on the side porch, or sometimes under the trees.
He just picks the spot where he wants to eat, and the maid brings out the table and dishes.
If she has to carry the food very far, he leaves her a dollar under the sugar bowl.
Jervie doesn't seem like a Pendleton at all.
He's so simple and sweet.
I know that seems like a funny way to describe a man, but it's true.
Unlike Julia, he doesn't care if people belong to the right sort of family.
He's extremely nice to the farmers around here.
They were suspicious of him at first, but now they like to talk to him.
It seems they didn't like his clothes very much!
I must say, his clothes are rather amazing.
He often wears white flannel trousers.
Just like a proper gentleman!
The other day we were going riding, and he came downstairs in fancy riding pants.
"Oh my!" Mrs. Semple walked around him and admired his clothes from every angle.
"Be careful where you sit.
You don't want to get those new clothes dirty."
Jervie rolled his eyes.
"Run along and do your work, Mrs. Semple.
You can't tell me what to do anymore. I've grown up."
"Why, Jervie Pendleton, you can't talk to me like that!"
Mrs. Semple pretended to be annoyed, but I could tell she was proud of him.
"I remember when I used to wash your face while you sat on my lap."
I burst out laughing.
I couldn't help myself!
"Why are you laughing?" they both said at once.
"He's so tall that it's hard to imagine him sitting on your lap!" I replied.
And he is tall, Daddy Longlegs.
Almost as tall as you.
"Well, he did," Mrs. Semple said.
"And you should have seen Mrs. Semple back then," Jervie said.
"She could run faster than I could!"
"So if he escaped from my lap, I could catch him!
Now run along, you two, I have work to do."
We've been having so many adventures.
We've explored the country for miles, and Jervie has even taught me how to fish.
August 28
We climbed Sky Hill yesterday afternoon.
That's a mountain near the farm.
There's no snow on the top.
It's not that high, but you're still pretty breathless when you reach the top.
"Let's stay and watch the sunset," Jervie said.
"We'll build a fire and cook our supper."
"I'd like to see the sun go down," I said.
"But I've never cooked outside before, never mind built a fire."
"Don't worry about a thing.
I'll do the cooking.
I'm used to camping."
So we had a delicious supper and watched the sunset.
We came back down the mountain by moonlight.
Fortunately, Jervie had a lantern, so we could find our way down the trail.
It was so much fun!
He laughed and joked and talked about such interesting things.
He has read all the books I've read, plus so many more.
It's amazing how many different things he knows.
September 3
I still haven't finished this letter!
Let me tell you what happened on Sunday morning.
"We must leave here by ten to get to church on time," Mrs. Semple said to Jervie.
"Very well, Mrs. Semple, you get the buggy ready," he replied.
"But if I'm not dressed, go without me."
"Oh, we'll wait," she said firmly.
"As you wish," he said.
"But don't keep the horses standing too long."
Then when she was dressing for church, he told me to change into my regular clothes.
We slipped out the back door and went fishing!
Did you ever hear anything so funny?
We cooked our fish over a campfire for lunch.
We didn't get home until four and then we went driving at five.
Mrs. Semple was disappointed that we didn't go to church.
She blamed herself for not training Jervie better when he was young.
But we think she was upset about something else—she wanted to show him off to her friends at church!
September 8
I'm sure you must move in the same social circles as Jervis Pendleton.
I wanted to ask him if he knew you.
But I couldn't because I don't know your real name.
You're Mr. Smith to me.
Isn't that silly?
I've been writing this letter for two weeks, so it's time I finally mailed it!
Affectionately,
Judy
September 10
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
School opens in about two weeks.
I'll be glad to start working again, although I've worked quite a bit this summer.
I wrote six short stories and seven poems.
I sent some to magazines, but they were all quickly rejected.
Jervie read a few of my stories when he was here.
He brought the mail in every day, so I couldn't hide the rejection letters from him.
"What's this, another rejection?" Jervie tossed a thick envelope at me.
I glanced at the return address.
It was from a magazine in New York. "Yep," I replied.
"Open it," Jervie said.
I opened the envelope and read the brief note.
"My story isn't quite right for them," I said.
"But I don't mind. Writing the story was good practice."
"Let me see your story."
Jervie took it and sat down in the parlor.
I paced in front of him while he read.
"I don't care that it was rejected," I mumbled.
"But I really hope you like it."
"Judy, this story is dreadful!" Jervie looked up at me.
"It's even worse than the last one you sent out.
You have absolutely no idea what you're talking about!
People don't act like this in the city!"
I laughed. "Don't worry about hurting my feelings!
Just blurt out the awful truth." I said, making a face at him.
What else could I do?
Jervie tried to hide a smile.
"What are you working on now?"
"A story set at college.
But I don't want to show it to you, if you're just going to make fun of it."
I snatched my story from his hand.
"At least you know something about college," he muttered.
"It might be more convincing than the one you sent to the magazine."
"Well, maybe I'll let you see it when I'm finished."
So a couple days later, I showed him my new story.
Amazingly, he liked it!
He had a secretary type it for me, and I sent it to a magazine.
But I haven't heard anything yet.
At least it wasn't rejected right away!
Jervie has gone back to New York City.
Everybody misses him, especially me.
I'm finding Mrs. Semple's conversation pretty boring.
Yours ever,
Judy
September 14
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
The postman just arrived with two letters for me.
The magazine accepted my story and will pay me fifty dollars.
I'm an AUTHOR!
The second letter is from the college.
I've won a scholarship that will pay for my tuition and board for two years.
The scholarship is for someone who has done exceptionally well in English and has also succeeded in other subjects.
I applied at the end of the school year.
But I was afraid I wouldn't get it because I'd failed those two exams my freshman year.
Now I won't be such a burden to you.
All I'll need is my monthly allowance.
I can probably make that amount writing or tutoring.
So I'll eventually be able to pay you back.
I can't wait for school to start!
Yours ever,
Jerusha Abbott, author of "When the Sophomores Won the Game"
September 26
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I'm back at college, where I am now a junior!
I'm rooming with Sallie and Julia again.
Our room is very nice this year.
Julia, who has an unlimited allowance, spent a lot of money on furniture and rugs.
I have been busy hemming curtains for our study, and welcoming back fifty dear friends.
I'm also unpacking two trunks full of clothes.
Quite a change from when I arrived here two years ago!
I received your letter—I mean, your secretary's letter.
I know you don't want me to pay you back.
But I want to do that.
And with this scholarship, I'll owe you less money than I once thought.
I don't understand your objections to the scholarship.
But it doesn't matter because I've already accepted the scholarship.
Affectionately,
Judy
September 30
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I can't believe you're still complaining about that scholarship.
I never knew such a stubborn man.
You say that I shouldn't accept gifts from strangers.
Well, what do you think you are?
I wouldn't know you if I met you on the street!
Besides, this scholarship isn't a gift.
It's more like a prize that I've earned.
I refuse to give up the scholarship.
And if you keep bothering me about it, I won't accept your allowance.
I'll spend endless hours tutoring freshmen.
You say that if I take the scholarship, I'm depriving another girl of an education.
If you care so much about educating girls, send another orphan to college!
I've given in to your demands in the past.
But this time I will stand FIRM.
Yours, with my mind completely made up,
Jerusha Abbott
November 9
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Julia Pendleton has invited me to visit her family for the Christmas holidays.
Can you imagine Jerusha Abbott of the John Grier Home dining with the rich people of New York?
I don't know why Julia wants me to visit.
But she seems quite attached to me lately.
To tell you the truth, I'd rather go to Sallie's house again.
But Julia asked me first, so I must go to New York.
I'm awed at the idea of meeting so many Pendletons at once.
I'll also need lots of new clothes.
So if you want me to stay at college, I'll happily do that.
Yours always,
Judy
December 7
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Thank you for permission to visit Julia.
I'm taking your silence to mean that I may go to New York for Christmas.
We've been in a social whirl here at college.
Last weekend was the Founder's Dance.
This was our first one because only juniors and seniors are allowed to go.
I invited Jimmy McBride.
Sallie invited his roommate at Princeton—the one who visited their summer house.
Bill is an awfully nice guy.
Julia invited a man from New York.
He was boring, but from one of the best families, of course.
Our guests arrived on Friday afternoon for tea.
Then they dashed to their hotel for dinner.
At half past seven, they returned for the dance.
Julia, Sallie, and I all had new dresses.
"That's the most beautiful dress I've ever seen!" I said to Julia as she took off her coat.
"Thank you. It came from Paris."
Julia twirled so we could admire every detail of her cream satin dress.
"I bet it cost a fortune!" Sallie whispered.
"Your dress is gorgeous too!" I said, admiring the pale blue fabric.
"We all look beautiful tonight!" Sallie took our hands, and we walked into the dance together.
Jimmy and his roommate were already there.
"Thank you for the beautiful flowers," I said to Jimmy.
I was carrying a small bouquet of red roses that he'd sent.
"Sallie told me what color to get," he admitted.
"They look very nice with your pink dress.
Now, tell me why the letters of the alphabet are hanging around the room."
"We wanted every girl to have a chance to dance," Sallie said.
"So we gave each one a list of partners.
After every dance you men should go and stand under the letter of your last name."
"That way your next partner can find you," I explained.
"So we're assigned a partner for every dance?" Jimmy gave Bill a look of dismay.
"No, not every dance," Sallie said.
"That's good!" Jimmy smiled at me.
Well, Jimmy McBride was a difficult guest!
Instead of waiting patiently with the other Ms, he wandered away to the Rs, or some other letter.
And then he sulked because he had to dance with so many girls.
"I only got to dance with you three times!" he complained at the end of the evening.
The next morning we had a concert.
I had written a funny song, and everyone seemed to like it.
After the concert, Jimmy and Bill found Sallie and me in the crowded room.
"How was the hotel?" Sallie asked.
"It was so full, we slept in rows on the pool tables," Bill joked.
"The next time I'm invited here, I'm bringing a tent," Jimmy said.
"And I'll pitch it right in the middle of campus."
"You wouldn't dare!" I said.
He laughed. "Just watch me."
"But we had a wonderful weekend, despite the crowded hotel," Bill assured us.
"The two of you must come to Princeton for our spring dance," Jimmy said.
Sallie and I looked at each other.
"Oh, yes!" we said together.
I hope you don't object to that, Daddy Longlegs.
It really sounds like so much fun.
Can I tell you something that I've recently discovered?
Do you promise not to think I'm vain?
I'm pretty.
Yours,
Judy
December 20
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I only have a moment to write.
I have to attend two classes, pack a suitcase, and catch the four o'clock train to New York.
But I couldn't leave without thanking you for my Christmas presents.
I love the necklace and the scarf and the gloves and handkerchiefs and books and purse.
Most of all, I love you!
But you shouldn't spoil me like this!
I now suspect that you're the kind trustee who donated the Christmas tree every year to the orphanage.
Were you also the trustee who made sure we had ice cream every Sunday?
That trustee was anonymous, but I recognize your kind touch.
You deserve to be happy for all the good things you do.
Merry Christmas,
Judy
January 11
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I meant to write to you from New York City, but I was so busy!
I had an interesting time at Julia's house.
But I'm glad I don't belong to such a family.
I'd really rather be an orphan!
I could hardly breathe in that house.
All the furniture was carved and upholstered and gorgeous.
But there was so much of it!
All the people were beautifully dressed and rich.
But I never heard one word of real conversation from the time we arrived until we left.
I don't think an idea ever entered the front door!
As for Julia's mother, all she ever talked about were jewels and dressmakers and social engagements.
So different from Mrs. McBride!
If I ever have a family, I'm going to use Mrs. McBride as my model.
I'll never let any of my children grow up like the Pendletons!
Maybe it's rude to criticize people you've been visiting.
If it is, please excuse me.
Don't tell anyone what I said about Julia's family.
This is all just between you and me.
I only saw Jervie once; he came for tea one afternoon.
I didn't have a chance to talk to him alone because Julia and her family were there.
"Hello, Miss Abbott," he said very formally.
"How nice to see you again, Mr. Pendleton," I replied.
Then we sat across the room from each other like we'd never met before!
It was so disappointing after our nice time last summer.
I'm not sure why he bothered to come at all.
The conversation was dreadful!
All about people I didn't know and places I'd never been.
"Jervis, have you seen any of the Thompson family this season?" Mrs. Pendleton asked.
"No."
"The Thompsons have such a lovely home on Fifth Avenue," she said to me.
"At the last ball I attended, Mrs. Thompson wore an exquisite gown.
It was trimmed with the most delicate lace I've ever seen.
And her new diamond necklace—how it sparkled!"
"It must have been very pretty," I mumbled.
I really didn't know what else to say.
I'm not used to talking about expensive jewelry.
As I sipped my tea, I looked at Jervie over the rim of my fine china cup.
I tried to catch his eye, but he was staring at the floor.
He looked miserable.
I don't think he likes his relatives very much.
And I know they don't like him!
"Such a strange young man!" Mrs. Pendleton said after Jervie left.
"It's hard to believe he's one of us.
I know he's my husband's brother, so I shouldn't say this but . . .
I really think there's something wrong with him."
I didn't know what to say to that!
But my silence didn't matter because Mrs. Pendleton went on talking.
"I don't know where he picked up some of his odd ideas.
He honestly thinks that everyone in the world should have the same amount of money.
Have you ever heard anything so ridiculous?"
"Well . . ." I started, but she talked over me.
"He throws away his money.
He's always trying to help the poor.
As if they could be helped!"
Well, that got a reaction from me!
"What do you think he should spend his money on?" I said loudly.
"Sensible things, of course!" Mrs. Pendleton replied.
"Yachts, automobiles, polo ponies!
The kinds of things that all young men spend their money on."
I didn't think it was her business how Jervie spent his money.
But I smiled because I knew of one thing he'd bought—candy.
He'd sent boxes of chocolate to Julia and me for Christmas.
In New York I saw so many theaters and beautiful houses.
My head was a confused jumble of marble floors and fancy furniture.
I'm so glad to be back at college in my own room.
I like being a student!
The books and classes keep me alive.
If my mind gets tired, I can exercise in the gym or outdoors.
And I have lots of nice friends.
Some evenings we do nothing but talk, talk, talk.
We go to bed thinking we've solved all the world's problems.
And we do like to laugh at each other's jokes.
I think I've discovered the secret of happiness.
It's appreciating the little things in life, like talking with friends.
I'm going to enjoy every second of my life from now on!
Yours ever,
Judy
February 11
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Don't be insulted that this is so short.
It's not a letter.
It's just a note to say I'll write a letter when exams are over.
I have to do well to keep my scholarship!
Yours, studying hard,
Judy
March 5
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
You'll be happy to hear that I passed all my exams. Hooray!
Everybody has to take gym class this semester, so I'm learning to swim.
"I hear they're teaching swimming a new way," I said to Sallie.
We were sitting in our study, drinking tea.
"But before I can go to class, I need a bathing suit.
Where will I find one this time of year?"
Sallie stood up and went into her room.
She came back holding a blue wool bathing suit.
"Right here! I have an extra one." She passed it to me.
So with my "new" bathing suit, I started lessons the next week.
The pool is made of cement and marble.
It's a gift from a former student.
At the start of class, we all sat along the edge of the pool.
"Listen to me, girls," the instructor said.
"I'm going to explain our new swimming system.
But I need a volunteer."
She looked at the line of girls, dangling their feet in the water.
No one raised a hand to volunteer.
"All right, you!" She pointed to me.
I stood up, and she gave me a special belt to fasten around my waist.
Then she hooked a rope onto a ring at the back of the belt.
"As you can see, this rope is attached to a pulley up there."
The instructor pointed to the ceiling.
"I'll hold on to the other end of the rope and keep you from sinking.
Get into the water, please."
So I slid into the pool.
That pulley system would be wonderful if I had confidence in the instructor.
But I was afraid she wouldn't hold on tightly.
I kept looking at her, and as a result, I didn't make much progress.
There's always next week!
Yours,
Judy
April 24
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Spring has finally arrived!
You should see how beautiful the campus is.
I think you should come and see it for yourself.
You could also see me while you're here.
But you should tell me in advance when you're coming.
Last Friday Jervie dropped in again, but he chose an inconvenient time.
One of the freshmen came upstairs to say we had a visitor.
Julia was at class, and Sallie was packing her suitcase.
So I went downstairs and there he was, sitting on a sofa.
He was holding a small bunch of flowers, which he handed to me.
"These are so lovely!"
I buried my nose in the flowers and inhaled the sweet scent.
Jervie laughed. "Let's go walking and then we can have tea in town."
"Oh, Jervie, I can't. Sallie and I are about to leave for Princeton."
He looked disappointed.
"Princeton? Why are you going there?"
"Sallie's brother, Jimmy, and his roommate have invited us for the weekend.
We're going to attend a dance and a ball game."
"You're going all that way by yourselves?" Jervie frowned in a disapproving way.
"Oh no! Sallie's mother is coming along as our chaperone."
Jervie was still frowning, but there was nothing I could do about that.
"I'm really glad to see you," I said, "and these flowers are lovely.
But I have to run or we'll miss our train.
If you wait here, I'm sure Julia will be back from class in half an hour."
Jervie told me to have a good time, but somehow I don't think he meant it.
I didn't ask you if I could go because I was afraid you'd say no.
But everything was perfectly proper.
We got permission from the college to be away for the weekend.
We had a wonderful time, but there are too many details to tell you here.
You know, I do love writing to you.
Although I must confess, you're not the only man I write to.
There are two others!
Did you ever hear anything so shocking?
I've been receiving lovely, long letters this winter from Jervie.
My address is typewritten on the envelope, so Julia won't recognize his handwriting.
And every week or so, I get a letter from Jimmy at Princeton.
It's usually scrawled on yellow paper.
He writes my address on the envelope himself.
Apparently Jimmy doesn't care if Sallie knows he's writing to me.
I answer all my letters promptly whether written on fine stationery or lined paper.
Speaking of letters, I should put this one in the mail before dinner.
Affectionately,
Judy
P.S. You'll never guess the topic of my paper for sociology class.
It's about the care of children in orphanages.
The professor wrote the topics on cards and then handed them to us at random.
I almost laughed out loud when I saw mine.
I'm an expert on that subject!
June 4
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
We're very busy right now.
Exams start tomorrow.
The weather is so lovely, but there's no time to enjoy it.
Oh well. Vacation's coming.
We took a break from studying today to discuss our summer plans.
"I'm going to Europe again," Julia said.
I put down my pen. "Oh, you're so lucky!"
"I guess so.
But sometimes I get bored being away from my friends for the whole summer.
This will be my fourth trip."
I'd be happy to go on my first trip—or my tenth!
But I didn't want to act like I was jealous. Even though I was!
"I'm going to our summer house in the mountains." Sallie looked at me.
"I wish you were coming with me."
"So do I. But my guardian would never agree to that.
I didn't even dare to ask."
Julia looked at me.
"Are you going back to that farm in the middle of nowhere?"
"Yes, at the end of the summer.
But first I'm tutoring Mrs. Charles Paterson's daughters.
We'll be staying at their cottage at the beach."
"Mrs. Paterson is a friend of my mother's," Sallie explained to Julia.
"She met Judy at our house during Christmas vacation sophomore year.
You must have made a good impression," she said to me.
"Mrs. Paterson seems nice," I said.
"And she's generous.
She's paying me fifty dollars a month.
I'd be happy with twenty-five, but I wasn't going to say no to fifty!"
Julia shook her head.
"I'm glad I don't have to worry about money. It's so boring."
As soon as Julia left the room, Sallie rolled her eyes.
"It must be nice to be able to buy whatever you want."
I shrugged.
"Maybe money is boring, but I'm looking forward to earning some this summer.
I'm also eager to see the Semples and my favorite farm animals."
I must tell you one more thing, Daddy Longlegs.
Sallie's brother, Jimmy, and his roommate, Bill, are graduating from Princeton this week.
Sallie and I really wanted to go to the ceremony.
But we have exams that day.
A bitter disappointment!
I must stop writing and do some more studying.
Yours,
Judy
June 10
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
This is the hardest letter I've ever written.
But I've decided what I must do, so there's no turning back.
It's very generous of you to offer to send me to Europe this summer.
I was very tempted to say yes!
But then I took some time to think.
I can't refuse to take your money for college, and then accept it for travel.
Besides, I don't want to get used to too many luxuries.
A trip to Europe is definitely a luxury!
I want to go, but I don't need to go.
Sometimes it's hard to live with Julia and Sallie.
They think the world owes them everything they want.
But I know that's not true for me.
Thank you again for your nice offer.
Don't be angry with me for refusing.
I appreciate your kindness.
I really do.
But you've already done so much for me.
Yours,
Judy
June 14
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I'm at the beach with Mrs. Paterson and her two daughters.
I left college a few days earlier than I'd planned.
Here's what happened.
I was in the middle of exams when Jervie showed up again.
He took me to tea in town.
"I'm going to Europe this summer," he announced.
I laughed. "It sounds like all the Pendletons will be there.
Are you going with Julia and her family?"
"No, I'm going by myself."
"My guardian offered to send me to Europe with a lady who's chaperoning a group of girls."
I stirred some sugar into my tea.
"But I decided not to go."
"Oh, you shouldn't say no to an opportunity like that!
Seeing Europe is an important part of your education."
He grinned at me.
"I could arrange to be in Paris when you're there.
We could run away from the chaperone and have dinner at a nice French restaurant."
I laughed. "That's very tempting, but I can't go."
When I tried to explain why I couldn't go, he wouldn't listen.
"You're a silly, stubborn child!" Jervie said.
"You don't know what's good for you."
He kept insisting I go.
That made me so angry!
I don't like feeling forced to do something.
I was glad to finish our tea and get back to studying.
As soon as exams were over, I packed my bags and left for Mrs. Paterson's.
And now I'm here by the sea.
Yours,
Judy
P.S. I told Jervie about you.
He thinks you're my guardian and an old family friend.
He knows I'm an orphan, but I didn't dare mention the John Grier Home.
August 19
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Here I am at Mrs. Paterson's cottage by the sea.
My window looks out on the loveliest landscape.
Or seascape, I guess.
Water, rocks, and sky are all I can see.
Did I describe my job in my last letter?
Mrs. Paterson's older daughter, Marion, is starting college this fall.
I'm tutoring her in English, Latin, and algebra.
I'm also working on English and Latin with Florence, the younger daughter.
And what a job it is!
I don't know how Marion is going to succeed at college.
And Florence is hopeless!
Pretty, but not very bright.
On my first morning, Mrs. Paterson asked me to come into her study.
"I know you're the girls' tutor," Mrs. Paterson said.
"But I don't want you working them too hard."
"No, ma'am."
"I want them to spend most of the day outdoors.
Perhaps you can find a pretty place to set up your classroom."
"I'll try, ma'am.
But if Marion's going to start college, she'll need to concentrate."
"I'm sure you'll figure out what to do."
And with that Mrs. Paterson went back to reading a letter.
So I took the girls outside, and we tramped around until we found a spot hidden in the cliffs.
At first, even I had trouble concentrating.
Every time a ship passed by, I thought of sailing to Europe.
And I wondered what I was missing.
"I'll never understand any of this!"
Marion tossed her math book onto the ground.
"Mother is making me go to college, but I don't see why.
It's a girls' college too.
How am I supposed to find a husband there?"
"If you get an education, then you'll be able to work," I said.
Florence giggled, and Marion said, "Married women don't have time to work!"
I frowned at them.
"Don't you want to learn math and grammar?"
"I've got no use for math," Marion said.
"And grammar is boring!"
"I agree," Florence chimed in.
"I worry about you two," I murmured.
And it was true.
Their conversation is so boring.
But I suppose that won't matter if they marry boring men.
I've certainly met quite a few boring ones this summer!
Fortunately, I only have to tutor the girls for half the day.
By the way, I received a letter from Jervie.
It's quite a short letter from Paris.
He's still upset that I refused to follow his advice about going to Europe.
He says if he gets back in time, he'll see me for a few days at Lock Willow Farm.
(If he gets back in time!
Does he expect me to sit around, hoping he'll arrive?)
I think he'll forgive me for staying here this summer.
But I'll probably have to be very sweet and docile.
I also received a letter from Sallie.
She wants me to come to their summer house for two weeks in September.
Do I have to ask your permission to do that?
Or am I old enough to do what I want?
Never mind.
I know I'm old enough because I'm a college senior.
Having worked all summer, I feel like taking a vacation.
I want to see the mountains and the lake.
I want to see Sallie and her brother.
Jimmy is going to teach me to canoe. That'll be fun!
But here's my real motive for going to Sallie's.
I want Jervie to arrive at Lock Willow and find that I'm not there.
I know that's mean.
But I MUST show him that he can't tell me what to do.
The only person who can do that is you—and not all the time.
I'm off to the woods!
Yours ever,
Judy
September 6
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I'm at Sallie's summer house in the mountains.
I'm pleased to say that I've been here for five days.
By the time your letter arrived at Mrs. Paterson's cottage, I had already left.
So I couldn't go to Lock Willow as you ordered.
Mrs. Paterson forwarded your letter to me here.
If you want me to obey in the future, tell your secretary to write more quickly.
The woods are lovely, and so is the house.
The weather is delightful, and I enjoy spending time with the McBrides.
The whole world is wonderful. I'm very happy!
Oh, I have to stop writing.
Jimmy is calling me to go canoeing. Good-bye!
Yours,
Judy
P.S. I'm sorry to have disobeyed you.
But I'm curious about one thing.
Why are you so against my having a little fun?
I worked hard all summer tutoring those ridiculous girls.
I deserve a break.
In spite of all your faults, I still appreciate you.
October 3
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I'm back at school, and I'm a senior.
This year I'm the editor of the student magazine.
You'll never guess what was waiting for me when I arrived.
A letter from Jervis Pendleton!
He'd sent it to Lock Willow Farm.
But I wasn't there because I was at Sallie's summer house.
Mrs. Semple forwarded the letter to me at college.
Here's what Jervie had to say:
"I'm sorry, but I won't be able to get to Lock Willow.
I've accepted an invitation to go yachting with some friends.
I hope you had a nice summer and that you're enjoying the farm."
I don't know what he was trying to do.
He knew my plans had changed and that I wasn't at Lock Willow.
Julia had told him that I was in the mountains with Sallie.
You men should leave scheming to women.
We are much better at it!
I'm living with Sallie and Julia again.
Sallie was the first to arrive.
She helped me unpack my trunk.
My clothes are so stylish now.
It's hard to believe that three years ago I was living in an orphanage.
"You have so many pretty outfits this year."
Sallie was admiring a new blue skirt with matching jacket.
"I have a confession.
I copied Mrs. Paterson's wardrobe!"
"How did you manage that?" Sallie asked.
"I found an inexpensive dressmaker this summer."
I pulled a green gown from my trunk.
"This isn't an exact copy of Mrs. Peterson's dress, but I really like it."
"You'll look beautiful in that!" Sallie said.
"Thank you. I'm really pleased with the way my clothes turned out."
And I was really pleased—until Julia arrived.
Her trunk was full of the most beautiful dresses I've ever seen.
She showed us a rainbow-colored ball gown.
"That looks like something an angel would wear!" Sallie exclaimed.
"I found it in a little shop in France," Julia said.
"There are the most exquisite dress shops in Paris.
And the hat shops!"
She sighed at the memory. "They're wonderful!"
"I must go to Paris someday!" I said.
I suppose you think we're silly to fuss over clothes like this.
But I do love pretty dresses.
Speaking of clothes . . . the maid for our hallway wears a gingham apron.
Just like the dresses I used to wear at the orphanage!
I get a chill every time I see her.
I want to get her some new aprons.
Then I'll sink the blue ones in the lake!
Yours ever,
Judy
November 17
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I need some sympathy.
My literary career has had a setback.
All last winter I was writing a novel.
This summer I worked on it whenever I wasn't tutoring my two silly girls.
I finished it right before school started and sent it to a publisher.
Well, he just rejected it.
He noticed my return address and realized that I was still at school.
He suggested I concentrate on my studies.
Then I could try writing again after I graduate!
He criticized my plot, my dialogue, and my sense of humor.
And I thought I'd written the Great American Novel!
I researched it while I was at Julia's last Christmas.
But I guess two weeks wasn't long enough to capture the spirit of New York City.
So I burned my manuscript.
Every single page!
I went to bed last night totally dejected.
I felt like I would never become a writer.
I also thought you'd thrown away your money trying to educate me.
But then I woke up this morning with a wonderful new plot in my head!
I've been working on my characters all day.
I'm so happy to be writing again.
You have to admit I'm an optimist.
Affectionately,
Judy
December 17
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I had the strangest dream last night.
I went into a bookstore, looking for something to read.
"Do you like fiction or nonfiction?" the clerk asked me.
"I like them both.
You have so many books here, I don't know where to start."
"Let me show you our latest bestseller."
He handed me a new book with a red cover.
"Oh my!" I said in surprise.
The book was The Life and Letters of Judy Abbott.
The John Grier Home was pictured on the cover, and my photo was inside.
I bought the book and took it home.
Then I sat up half the night reading.
I was just about to find out my husband's name when I woke up!
By the way, my real book is going well.
I've finished four chapters and drafted five more.
I'll be a great writer yet. Just watch me!
Yours affectionately,
Judy
December 26
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Do you have any sense at all?
You shouldn't give me 17 Christmas presents!
That's too many.
What if we argued?
I'd have to hire a moving van to return all your gifts.
I'm sorry the necktie I sent was so crooked.
I made it myself.
But I guess you could tell that by looking at it.
You'll have to wear it on cold days and keep your coat buttoned up.
Thank you a thousand times for my gifts. I like them all!
Merry Christmas,
Judy
P.S. Here's a four-leaf clover to bring you luck in the New Year.
I found it last summer at the McBrides' house.
January 9
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Would you like to do something that will guarantee you get into heaven?
There's a family in town in desperate need of help.
I know the oldest daughter, who's 24.
She's a seamstress and sometimes makes clothes for girls at the college.
I went to her house today to pick up a skirt, and she was in tears.
"What's wrong, Emily?" I asked.
"Oh, everything, Miss Abbott."
She wiped her eyes with a handkerchief.
"My father used to work at the glass factory.
But he got ill and was sent to a hospital.
That took all our savings.
Now I'm the only one supporting our family."
"Don't you have anyone who can help you?" I asked.
She shook her head sadly.
"My two older brothers are working.
But we don't know where they are.
They haven't sent any money home.
My mother doesn't have a job, and my three younger siblings aren't old enough to work."
I didn't want to embarrass her, but I had to ask a question.
"Would you mind telling me how much money you make?"
"I make dresses and do other sewing for a dollar and a half a day.
At night I embroider table linens.
But I don't have work every day."
During this conversation, Emily's mother had been sitting quietly.
But now she spoke up.
"Things will work out," Emily's mother said.
"Don't worry about us, miss."
Emily shook her head.
"I don't know how we're going to get through this winter."
"Let me see what I can do," I said.
"I might be able to help you."
I was shaking my head in disbelief when I left Emily's house.
Her mother just sits there all day while Emily kills herself working!
You're the richest man I know.
Do you think you could spare one hundred dollars?
This girl deserves help a lot more than I ever did.
One hundred dollars would buy some coal for the heater and shoes for the little children.
Can you imagine being without shoes in the winter?
It would also give Emily a financial cushion.
Then she wouldn't worry on days when she has no work.
Meanwhile . . . my least favorite class is philosophy.
The professor seems to think this is our only class.
He piles on the work!
He tries to lighten his dreary lectures with jokes.
But they aren't funny at all.
Where do you think my new novel is?
In the wastebasket! I could tell it was terrible.
So I knew it would never get published.
January 10
I'm writing to you from a bed of pain.
I have swollen tonsils.
I can swallow hot milk, but that's it.
The doctor visited me in the infirmary.
"Why didn't you have your tonsils removed when you were a child?" he asked.
"What were your parents thinking?"
"I have no idea, but they weren't thinking about me."
I didn't actually say that because it hurt too much to talk.
But that's what I wanted to say.
Yours,
J.A.
January 12
Dear Mr. Philanthropist,
Your check for Emily's family came today.
Thank you so much!
I skipped gym class and took it to her right after lunch.
You should have seen Emily's face!
She was so surprised and happy and relieved.
She looked almost young again.
(It's pitiful that she looks so old at 24.)
"Good things are starting to happen," Emily said.
"This morning a woman ordered a wedding dress and all the clothes for her honeymoon.
That's two months' worth of work.
And now this check arrives!"
"I told you everything would work out," her mother said.
I tried to stay quiet, but I'd lost my patience with her.
"Things didn't just happen to work out," I said.
"They worked out because I told Mr. Smith about your problems.
And he very kindly decided to write a check."
"Yes, Mother," Emily said.
"It's Miss Abbott and Mr. Smith that we should be thanking."
Yours most gratefully,
Judy Abbott
P.S. My throat is feeling much better.
I'm out of bed and back to school. Obviously!
February 15
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
This morning we had a guest minister at chapel.
It doesn't matter where a preacher comes from or what church he belongs to.
He always has the same message for us.
I was sitting next to Sallie, hoping to hear an inspiring sermon.
But instead he preached the same old thing.
"Young ladies, you must be careful not to get too much education.
You must not waste too much time reading or thinking."
The minister looked out at the pews filled with girls.
We had just finished exams, so we'd done a lot of reading and thinking.
The minister went on.
"Your main role in life is to be a wife and mother.
Too much education harms a woman."
I shook my head in disbelief.
Of course I'd like to be a wife and mother.
But I want to do something more with my life.
I want to be a great author!
"I wonder if he speaks at men's colleges," I whispered to Sallie.
"Do you think he warns men that too much education will harm them?"
Sallie stifled a giggle.
"I doubt it, but he should!"
Here's some news: We no longer have to turn out our lights at ten o'clock.
We can stay up all night if we want!
The only rule is that we can't disturb others.
No loud parties.
So what do you think is the result?
Are we all staying up until dawn?
No, just the opposite.
At nine o'clock everyone is tired and starting to think about bed.
It's nine thirty now, so time to say goodnight.
Yours,
Judy
March 5
Dear Mr. Trustee,
Tomorrow is the first Wednesday of the month—always an exhausting day at the John Grier Home.
Everyone will be relieved when it's time for you trustees to leave.
By the way, did you ever pat me on the head when I was a little orphan?
Please give the orphanage my love.
I really mean that.
It's been almost four years since I lived there, and I've come to appreciate it.
When I started college, I resented that I'd been robbed of a normal childhood.
I envied the other girls when they talked of home and family.
But now I think it's an advantage that I was brought up in an orphanage.
I see the world from a unique perspective.
The other girls—especially Julia—don't realize how happy their lives are.
But I'm thankful every minute that I'm happy.
And I've vowed to keep on being happy.
Give my regards to Mrs. Lippett.
(I think "regards" expresses how I feel toward her. "Love" is too strong a word.)
Remember to tell her how nicely I've turned out.
Affectionately,
Judy
April 4
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Sallie and I are spending Easter vacation at Lock Willow Farm.
We were in desperate need of some peace and quiet.
"It's so relaxing here," Sallie said as soon as we arrived.
"I didn't think I could eat another meal in our dining hall."
"Me neither," I replied.
"It's so exhausting to dine with four hundred girls, especially when you're feeling tired.
You can't even hear the girl across the table unless she shouts."
"And that just adds to the noise!"
Sallie and I have been taking long walks every day.
This morning we climbed to the top of Sky Hill.
That's the mountain where Jervie and I once cooked supper.
It's hard to believe that was almost two years ago.
I could still see where the smoke from our fire blackened some rocks.
"You're awfully quiet," Sallie said.
"What are you thinking about?"
"Oh, nothing. I was just admiring the view."
It's funny how certain places get connected with certain people.
Whenever you see that place, you think of that person.
Suddenly I missed Jervie very much—for about a minute!
But I couldn't say anything to Sallie.
I've never said much to her—or Julia!—about Jervie.
Sallie and I are also spending part of our vacation reading and writing.
Nothing too serious.
We're just reading novels and writing letters.
Oh, but I have started to write a new book!
I began working on it three weeks ago.
I think I finally understand what Jervie and that editor were trying to tell me.
You have to write about things you know.
Otherwise the story doesn't feel authentic.
So guess where my novel is set?
The John Grier Home!
It's about the little things that happen every day in an orphanage.
It's really very good.
I'm going to finish this book and get it published.
If you want something and try hard enough, you'll eventually get it.
I really believe that.
I've been trying for four years to get a letter from you.
And I haven't given up hope yet!
Affectionately,
Judy
May 17
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
This letter will be very short.
My hand aches from taking notes in class and writing my novel.
Graduation is in three weeks.
I think you should come and introduce yourself to me.
Julia is inviting Jervie, and Sallie's inviting Jimmy.
But who can I invite?
Just you and Mrs. Lippett, and I don't want her here.
Please come. I'll hate you if you don't.
Yours, with love and writer's cramp,
Judy
June 19
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
I'm officially a college graduate!
My diploma is in the bottom drawer of my bureau here at Lock Willow with my two best dresses.
I was disappointed that you weren't at the graduation ceremony.
But thank you for the roses. They were lovely.
We were getting dressed for the ceremony when they arrived.
"Another box of flowers for you, Judy!" Sallie said.
"That makes three. One from Jimmy.
One from Jervis. And now this one."
"You get more flowers than anyone I know."
Julia peeked over my shoulder, trying to see who they were from.
I read the card and announced, "These are from my guardian, Mr. Smith."
"I still don't understand why Uncle Jervis sent you roses," Julia went on.
I smiled to myself. "Probably just because I'm your roommate."
"I'm Julia's roommate too, and he didn't send me flowers," Sallie said.
"Not that I need any more flowers.
Jimmy's are enough for me.
Whose flowers are you going to carry in the procession, Judy?"
"Oh, I hadn't thought about that."
Julia had already moved on to other things.
"I hate these horrible black caps and gowns we have to wear.
What's the point of a new dress if it's hidden?"
"I think we're all supposed to look alike." Sallie turned to me.
"Have you decided on your flowers?
We have to leave in a few minutes."
"Yes, I'll carry Mr. Smith's and put the others in some water in the bathtub."
And so, Mr. Smith, it was your roses that had the honor of accompanying me to graduation.
I only wish you had been there to see me.
I'm at the farm for the summer—maybe forever.
All I want are peace and quiet and lots of time to write.
And I have that here.
Jervie is coming for a week or so in August.
Jimmy McBride is going to drop by sometime this summer.
I wish you would arrive in your car, but I know that's a hopeless dream.
Sincerely yours,
Judy Abbott, B.A.
P.S. Aren't you proud to see bachelor of arts after my name?
It looks so official.
July 24
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
It's so much fun to work.
(Maybe you don't know that.
Do you even work at all?)
It's especially fun when you're doing something that makes you happy.
Every day I write as fast as my pen can go.
My only problem is that there aren't enough hours in the day to work on my book.
Did I tell you that Amos, the farmhand, married Carrie, the maid, in May?
I think marriage has ruined their relationship.
The other day he tracked mud on the floor.
"Look what you've done, Amos!" Carrie scolded him.
"I just washed that floor!"
She used to laugh when he did something like that.
"Go back outside and bring in some wood for the fire," Carrie said.
Amos grumbled something I couldn't hear.
He used to do anything she asked, but no more.
Looking at them, I vowed never to marry.
Jimmy McBride came for dinner last Sunday.
I was so glad to see him.
He reminded me that there's a whole world beyond this farm.
Jimmy travels around selling bonds to banks.
"How did it go with the bank in town?"
I asked as we sat down to dinner.
"They weren't interested in the bonds at all." Jimmy sighed.
"I'm not having much luck as a salesman."
I think he's too nice to be successful in the financial world.
"If this job doesn't suit you, perhaps you could work for your father," I said.
"That's the last thing I want to do!"
Jimmy seemed so unhappy about his job.
I'm glad he enjoyed Mrs. Semple's fried chicken and ice cream.
The postman has just brought us some news.
Jervie will arrive next Friday and spend a week here.
That's something to look forward to.
But I'm afraid my poor book will suffer.
Jervie is a very time-consuming guest.
Yours as always,
Judy
September 19
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Something has happened, and I need some advice.
Would it be possible for me to see you?
It's so much easier to talk than write.
Also I don't want your secretary reading my letter.
Judy
P.S. I'm very unhappy.
October 3
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
You wrote me a note!
And it's in your own handwriting, which looks pretty wobbly.
I'm sorry that you've been sick.
I wouldn't have bothered you if I'd known.
Yes, I'll tell you my problem in a letter, but it's VERY PRIVATE.
Please burn this after you read it.
Before I begin, here's a check for one thousand dollars.
It seems funny to be sending you a check!
I still owe you two thousand dollars, but I intend to repay that.
Where do you think I got the money?
A publisher has bought my book!
You probably think I'm wild with joy.
But I'm not, because of my problem.
I'm in love with Jervis Pendleton.
We're so compatible in every way.
We can talk for hours, and we have the same sense of humor.
He's 14 years older than I am, but sometimes he seems like a boy.
He still needs someone to remind him to wear his raincoat!
I wish you could meet him and see how wonderful he is.
The whole world seems empty without him.
I hate the moonlight because he's not here to enjoy it with me.
So what's my problem?
One day when he was here at the farm, we went for a long walk and a picnic.
We had just finished our lunch, when Jervie announced that he had a question for me.
He seemed awfully nervous, but he got right to the point.
Jervie took my hand and asked, "Judy, will you marry me?"
"Oh, Jervie!" I said softly.
He smiled at me.
I know he thought I was pleased.
And I was happy.
But I was also miserable because there was no way I could marry him.
"Oh, Jervie," I said again.
"I'm so sorry, but I can't marry you."
"What do you mean?" His face clouded over.
I just sat on the grass, silent and miserable.
"It's that Jimmy McBride," he said angrily.
"Do you want to marry him?"
I shook my head no, but I know Jervie didn't believe me.
(I'd never marry Jimmy in a million years. He's not grown-up enough.)
"I can't believe what a foolish girl you are, Judy Abbott!"
Now I was angry.
"Don't call me a foolish girl!
How dare you presume that I'd marry you!"
And then we both said some dreadful, hurtful things.
We quickly packed up our picnic basket and returned to the farmhouse.
Jervie left that afternoon, and I haven't heard from him since.
I couldn't tell him the truth.
I refused his proposal because I love him so much.
I know that sounds absurd.
But I was afraid he'd regret marrying me, and I couldn't stand that.
You see, he knows I'm an orphan.
But I've never told him about the orphanage.
It didn't seem right for someone of his background to marry someone like me.
Who knows what my original family is like?
They could be perfectly DREADFUL people.
But there's another reason.
You've spent all this money to educate me as a writer.
So I should at least give that a try—although I guess I could be a wife and a writer too.
This all happened about two months ago.
I hadn't heard a word from Jervie since he was here.
I was getting used to having a broken heart.
But then I got a letter from Julia and that stirred me up again.
She casually mentioned that her uncle Jervis got sick while traveling in Canada.
He has been ill ever since with pneumonia.
And I never even knew it!
I imagine Jervie is pretty unhappy, and I know I am!
What if I go to him and explain that the trouble isn't Jimmy McBride, but the John Grier Home?
Would that be a terrible thing to do?
You know a lot about the world, and you probably have a family.
So I'd like your unemotional opinion on this mess.
Yours,
Judy
October 6
Dear Daddy Longlegs,
Thank you for inviting me to visit you.
I'll arrive next Wednesday at half past four.
I laughed when you asked if I could find the way.
Of course I can!
I've been to New York City before to visit Julia.
I can't believe that I'll finally get to meet you.
Sometimes I don't think that you're a real person.
You're very nice to invite me when you aren't feeling well.
Take good care of yourself.
I've just had an awful thought.
Do you have a butler?
I'm afraid of butlers.
If one opens the door, I'll faint right there on your steps.
Affectionately,
Judy
P.S. You've never told me your real name.
When I arrive, should I ask for Mr. Smith?
Thursday Morning
My Very Dearest Jervie-Daddy-Longlegs Pendleton-Smith,
Did you sleep last night? I didn't.
I was too excited and happy.
I don't think I'll ever sleep again!
But you must sleep, so that you can get well and visit me.
Yesterday was the most wonderful day of my life.
If I live to be 99, I'll never forget the tiniest detail.
The girl who left Lock Willow Farm yesterday morning was very different from the one who returned.
It was still dark when Mrs. Semple called me.
"Judy! It's half past four.
Time to wake up!
You've got a big day ahead of you."
I quickly got dressed and ran downstairs for breakfast.
"Are you excited about going to New York City?"
Mrs. Semple poured me a cup of coffee.
"Oh, yes! I'm going to see Daddy Longlegs!"
"Daddy Longlegs?" Mrs. Semple looked surprised.
"I mean Mr. Smith." I'd never told her my nickname for you.
I took the train to New York City.
When I arrived at your house, it looked so big and intimidating.
I didn't even dare to knock.
So I walked around the block to work up my nerve.
But I shouldn't have been afraid.
Your butler was such a nice, fatherly old man.
He made me feel right at home.
"Is this Miss Abbott?" he said right away.
So I didn't have to ask for Mr. Smith after all.
"Yes," I replied.
"He'll be very glad to see you."
Your butler nodded.
"Please wait here."
As I waited, I kept saying to myself, "I'm going to see Daddy Longlegs!
I'm going to see Daddy Longlegs!"
Soon the butler returned. "Please come upstairs to the library, miss."
I could barely contain my excitement as I followed him.
Outside the library door, the butler turned to me.
"He's been very ill, miss," the butler whispered.
"This is the first day he's been allowed to sit up.
You won't stay too long?
The doctor doesn't want him to get overexcited."
I could tell that your butler is very fond of you.
Then he knocked and said, "Miss Abbott is here."
I went into the library, and the door closed behind me.
The room was quite dim compared to the brightly lit hallway.
For a moment I could barely make out anything.
Then I saw a big easy chair in front of the fire.
There was a tea table with a smaller chair beside it.
I realized that a man was sitting in the big chair, propped up with pillows.
He had a blanket over his knees.
He started to stand up.
"Oh, please don't trouble yourself," I said. "Sit down."
But the man stood—rather shakily—and steadied himself with the chair.
He just looked at me without a word.
My hands flew to my face in amazement.
"Oh, Jervie! You're here!" I cried.
"Did Mr. Smith ask you to come?"
Then you laughed and held out your hand.
"My dear Judy," you said as I took your hand.
"Didn't you guess the truth? I am Daddy Longlegs."
"What?" In an instant I realized what was going on.
I sank onto a chair, heat flooding my face.
"Oh, I've been so stupid!
There were a hundred little clues, if I'd been paying attention."
I shook my head.
"I guess I wouldn't make a very good detective."
Jervie was grinning at me. "No, but I love you anyway."
"I love you too!"
You paused for a moment to steady yourself.
"I can't go down on one knee, but will you marry me?"
This time I didn't have to say no.
"Of course, Jervie!"
We spent a wonderful half hour together before your doctor came in.
"Please don't tire him, miss," the doctor said as he led me from the room.
"Though I must say you've done him a world of good.
He looks ten years younger."
I was so dazed that I could barely find my way to the train station.
And then I almost took a train for St. Louis!
You were pretty dazed yourself.
You forgot to give me tea!
But we're both so happy.
This morning I've been out walking to all the places we've been together.
I wish you were here to climb the hills with me.
I'm missing you dreadfully, Jervie dear.
But it's a happy kind of missing.
We'll soon be together for the rest of our lives.
At last I belong to someone.
That's a new feeling for me, and it's very sweet indeed.
Yours forever and ever,
Judy
P.S. This is the first love letter I've ever written.
I hope you like it.
